papers.title: Highly Deformable Proprioceptive Membrane for Real-Time 3D Shape Reconstruction
papers.summary: Reconstructing the three-dimensional (3D) geometry of surfaces is essential for robot perception and physical interaction. Vision-based approaches reconstruct surfaces at high resolution from an external viewpoint but often require a clear line of sight. A conformable membrane that reconstructs its own deformation offers a complementary route. Based on optical waveguide shape sensing, this work presents a stretchable proprioceptive silicone membrane that reconstructs localized contact and in-plane stretching under large deformation. The membrane integrates edge-mounted light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and centrally distributed photodiodes (PDs) in an elastomeric waveguide using liquid-metal interconnects. A neural network maps the optical intensity measurements to a dense point cloud of the membrane surface. Optical acquisition and model inference run in real time at about 90~Hz. Under localized pressing of up to about 25~mm depth, the membrane achieves an overall shape reconstruction error of 1.580~mm. It also localizes finger contacts with a mean error of 1.779~mm. Extreme strain tests show that the optical signals remain informative for in-plane outline reconstruction up to 75\% strain, approaching the mechanical limit of the liquid-metal circuit. These results indicate a practical route to proprioceptive shape sensing in deformable robotic systems.

papers.title: PACE-WM: Parallel World Modeling with Action History for Visual Planning
papers.summary: JEPA-style world models support visual planning by predicting future representations conditioned on future actions. However, similar observations can conceal different motion states, making temporal context essential for interpreting future action effects. We propose PACE-WM, a parallel world model that uses executed-action history to contextualize future prediction and planning. Specifically, PACE-WM maintains a recurrent memory of executed actions and uses this memory to condition a causal Transformer. PACE-WM predicts multiple future representations in parallel without recursive predicted-state feedback within each prediction window. We further introduce Reference-Anchored Minimum Progress (RAMP) for action selection during planning. RAMP scores candidate actions by their predicted goal improvement along direct and split paths relative to a shared reference. Across four visual planning tasks, PACE-WM with RAMP achieves an average success rate of $98\%$ and plans approximately $7$-$9\times$ faster than autoregressive LeWM under matched CEM settings. We also construct four controlled benchmarks to evaluate PACE-WM's capabilities in motion disambiguation, goal-relative motion, and goal adaptation. papers.title: From Acting to Learning: Experience Selection toward Continually Learning Agents
papers.summary: Successful agent interactions provide training data, but success alone does not determine which records a student should learn from. papers.title: Simulation-Based Testing of RCM-Constrained Robotic Software via Task Manifolds
papers.summary: System-level testing of surgical robots requires generating executable test scenarios that exercise diverse, safety-critical behaviors. However, remote-center-of-motion (RCM) surgical manipulators operate within tightly constrained workspaces governed by coupled task geometry, inverse kinematics, and motor limits. Direct sampling in motor-command or Cartesian spaces frequently wastes testing budgets on physically unfeasible configurations. To address this limitation, we present a manifold-centered testing framework that decouples feasible test-domain construction from downstream test-generation strategies. Candidate inputs are generated directly within this constructed feasible domain and mapped to lower-level joint commands for simulation execution. Offline trajectory safety oracles and a spatial reference grid then evaluate failure yield and coverage. We compare our task-manifold representation against Cartesian XYZ and principal component analysis (PCA) under random testing, systematic traversal, and genetic search strategies. Results demonstrate that the feasible task domain improves test-generation efficiency and enables systematic reference-cell coverage. Crucially, random and genetic search strategies detect a broader spectrum of failure patterns than baseline representations, revealing that complete reference-cell coverage alone does not exhaust intra-cell behavioral dynamics. Furthermore, differential testing between defective and patched controller versions reveals that targeted evolutionary search detects aggregate failure-rate shifts from software repairs. Finally, a cross-platform study on a 7-DoF Kinova Gen3 arm in MoveIt 2 confirms workflow transferability to kinematically redundant manipulators. Together, these findings highlight the necessity of combining feasibility-aware domain modeling with complementary search strategies for systematic testing of robot software.

papers.title: OpenRing: Deadlock-Free Execution of Any Planner on AGV Floors with One-Way Lanes
papers.summary: Lifelong multi-agent path finding replans routes for automated guided vehicles, but deviations can invalidate a plan. With one-way lanes, a late vehicle or lost planner can close a ring of full segments. We separate how fast the floor runs from whether it keeps running. In OpenRing a planner proposes routes and an order, a local guard commits only moves and route changes that cannot close such a ring, and the order binds for a bounded time. Despite arbitrary proposals or planner loss, no ring closes. With two-place segments, traffic can continue under disturbances; progress is guaranteed once they end, and all vehicles exit if entries also stop. Among rules that reroute only on a proposal, every guard veto is necessary, and a clean plan keeps its crossing orders. The guarantee has a price: no rule that never stores a vehicle in a crossing under arbitrary stops carries more than $B/T_s$ per segment of $B$ places and traversal time $T_s$. With binding orders, three planners deadlock in 80 of 126 runs across eight floors. Inside OpenRing, none of the 126 runs deadlocks. OpenRing's closed-loop throughput rivals or exceeds the best baseline's. Physics simulations show no deadlocks or overlaps.

papers.title: Flying over The Uncertain Nature (FORTUNE): Intelligent and Humanistic 3D Path Planning for Low-Altitude Collaboration
papers.summary: Low-altitude intelligent agents are driving demand for timely, socially responsible collaborative sensing in dynamic urban environments. Yet jointly handling heterogeneous spatio-temporal sensing demands, real-time uncertainty, and human-centered constraints in a unified multi-uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) framework remains challenging. We study 3D multi-UAV path planning and joint task assignment under heterogeneous spatio-temporal uncertainty of ground points of interest (PoIs). Unlike studies assuming static, known PoIs, we formulate a unified model capturing persistent (Type-I), temporally predictable (Type-II), and emergent unpredictable (Type-III) demands. Following the low-altitude-for-good principle, we explicitly model altitude-dependent societal and environmental costs, including noise and public safety risks, jointly optimizing sensing effectiveness and socially compliant operations. To solve the resulting large-scale mixed-integer nonlinear problem, we propose FORTUNE, a hierarchical offline-online framework. Offline, a Transformer-based predictor forecasts Type-II activation windows, while an enhanced sparrow search algorithm (ES2A) with priority-aware decoding and danger-aware evolution generates globally coordinated flight plans. Online, lightweight trajectory refinement accommodates new Type-III PoIs while preserving global mission coherence. Experiments on real-world traffic and synthetic datasets show FORTUNE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks, validating effectiveness, scalability, and practical applicability in dynamic low-altitude systems.

papers.title: Geo-Force: A Theory of Force Sensing from Object Geometry
papers.summary: Robots need contact forces to handle delicate objects, but tactile sensors are fragile and hard to integrate, whereas depth sensors, such as RGB-D cameras, are widely available. A virtual touch sensor that keeps the sensing surface of a tactile sensor but replaces its electronics with a touch signal predicted from the target object's geometry, as measured by a depth sensor, could close this gap, yet it is unclear what such a virtual sensor computes and when its output can be trusted. We give a formal answer. We define the Geometric Force as the force on each taxel of a virtual touch sensor, computed in three steps: rendering the surface to be touched as seen from the virtual sensor, predicting the touch signal with a touch map, learned or simulated, and estimating the force from that signal. We prove three properties of the Geometric Force. First, its force vectors only rotate under a change of coordinate frame. Second, it vanishes when the rendered surface does not touch the virtual sensor. Third, it is stable: its error grows at most linearly with the errors of the three steps for Lipschitz maps. The rendering error, in turn, depends on how well the surface is sampled or reconstructed and how accurately the sensor is placed. We then show a fundamental limit: geometry does not reveal the object's stiffness, so no touch map can predict touch exactly for objects of the same shape and different stiffness. Under an elastic contact model, all object-specific knowledge resides in the touch map. From these results, we derive requirements on the depth sensor and the objects, design rules, and the conditions under which such a virtual sensor fails.

papers.title: Mechanistic Analysis of Unified Proximity-Tactile Observation by a Capacitive Fingertip Array Constrained by a Metal Phalanx
papers.summary: A capacitive fingertip array on a metal phalanx under thin silicone skin senses centimetre-scale conductive targets by fringing fields and contact force by dielectric compression. Electrode-to-body parasitics exceed the useful proximity increment by one to three orders of magnitude, and crosstalk and time-division-multiplexing (TDM) settling prevent identifying the capacitance-to-digital converter (CDC) reading with the electrode-target capacitance. The array is modelled as a multi-conductor system (sensing electrodes, driven-shield nodes, phalanx ground and an external target). The CDC measurand follows from the Maxwell capacitance matrix, with each inactive termination in the observation operator. Three mechanisms are examined: driven-shield hiding of shield-branch current and gain/phase-mismatch leakage; distinct far- and near-field operators; and TDM settling as a frame-rate limit set by shield load. A single layer used for both proximity and force reads Delta C = Delta C_force + Delta C_dielectric(epsilon_target), so its force map cannot be material-independent. A dual-array stack is analysed: the outer array is grounded as a Faraday screen during contact, and the inner array reads silicone-gap compression. FEM simulations give a monotonic, nonlinear contact response (4.6 fF at 0.05 mm to 370 fF at 0.5 mm on a 1.08 pF base), a nylon-versus-metal difference of at most 0.3 fF at exported-matrix resolution (not mesh-converged), mutual-term cancellation under driven-shield readout, and about 1 fF crosstalk on the coarse mesh. In proximity mode, electrode-shield coupling of 1.47 pF makes 10^{-3}-10^{-4} mismatch a quantitative gate: a 15.9 fF increment at 5 mm equals the leakage at |epsilon_A| ~ 10^{-2}. Force map, mechanical crosstalk and all bench quantities remain unvalidated; the equations and FEM evidence are a baseline for prototype calibration, not measured performance claims.

papers.title: Perceive Once, Escalate on Demand: Handing Off Visual KV Memory from Small to Large VLMs
papers.summary: An embodied agent cannot afford a large vision-language model (VLM) at every step of a long video, so a cascade runs a small VLM continuously and escalates only uncertain decisions to a large one. Each escalation, however, forces the large model to re-encode a history the small model has already perceived, and this dominates its cost. We present Baton, which hands the large model the small model's visual memory, its key-value (KV) cache over the history. Baton rests on one finding: the large model needs a usable memory, not a faithful copy of its own. A map trained to reproduce the large model's cache matches it most closely, yet brings no gain over the small model alone. Baton instead distills a per-layer linear map, without labels, from the large model's own answers, with the large model encoding only the current frame. Interventions on the map trace the gain to one direction, carried by the middle third of the large model's layers. On RoboMME, Baton beats the small model alone, a pruned or shortened re-watch, and a text memory; as the escalation channel of a cascade it matches re-watching to within about one point at 28-47% less compute, and 8x less per escalation at 64 frames. Its gain grows with the large model, from 8B to 32B, tracks the large model's headroom across eight model pairs from four families, and transfers zero-shot to OpenEQA.

papers.title: Staleness Deadlines for Motion Plans during Onboard Reasoning
papers.summary: Language models may enable general autonomy in robot planning, but onboard their reasoning can run for most of a minute while the robot and nearby pedestrians keep moving. The robot must then decide how long to follow a plan that the pending answer may overturn. Here we present staleness deadlines, which hand that decision to the robot's clock. Calibrated prediction regions for pedestrians and deviation tubes for the robot set the deadline. When the language model answers, a graph planner rebuilds the route, which the robot adopts only after it passes the same clearance check against walls and predicted pedestrians. Exact binomial tests determine which prespecified budget-selection policies keep close calls, wrong decisions and late arrivals below their targets at each inference profile. Candidate policies either fix one budget or set each query's budget from how long the robot can continue its plan before it must brake. We study corridor signs that close routes and delivery requests whose destination the language model must infer. In 81,000 simulated missions with recorded Qwen3-4B answers, full reasoning cuts wrong decisions about twentyfold, and tracking until the deadline cuts late arrivals by up to 64%. The robot never collides while it moves, although pedestrians who never yield still walk into the stopped robot in 23% of offline and 32% of live missions. On a Jetson AGX Orin under perception load, short budgets fail the wrong-decision target, and full reasoning the lateness target. Between these extremes, a fixed-budget policy passes for corridor signs and per-query policies pass for deliveries. Live Orin runs match offline replay on all three losses in 24 of the 32 missions where either run records a loss. The deadline turns slower reasoning into measurable mission outcomes, which let designers test how much reasoning each inference profile can support.

papers.title: LoCo-WAM: Test-Time Training as Long Context for World-Action Models
papers.summary: World-action models guide robot actions by predicting what happens next, but typically condition on a short observation history. Extending this history increases computation at every decision and can require a separately trained model. We introduce LoCo-WAM, which learns from the outcomes of its actions through test-time training while keeping the same short history length. It uses newly observed frames to update a low-rank adapter in the video expert, whose adapted predictions guide subsequent actions. The updates accumulate within each episode and are reset between episodes, allowing past observations to influence decisions after they leave the input window. LoCo-WAM thus learns from a longer stream of experience without expert action labels, additional data or meta-training. Experiments on two world-action models show improved task success across four simulation benchmarks. On RoboCasa GR-1, a model with 2.4,s of history matches one trained with 9.6,s, while a model with 4.8,s exceeds it by 4.8 percentage points. Our analysis shows that the updates improve prediction of upcoming frames, affect the action mainly through adaptation of the imagined future, and have an increasing effect on actions as the episode unfolds.

papers.title: 3D Open-Vocabulary Detection via Visual Alignment and Generative Captions
papers.summary: Open-vocabulary 3D object detection remains a significant challenge for outdoor scenes, with existing methods often struggling to effectively transfer the rich semantic knowledge from powerful 2D Vision-Language Models (VLMs) into a 3D context. We generate class-agnostic 3D proposals to source regions from the entire scene, without relying on any manual labels. We leverage a spatially-aware VLM to extract a semantic embedding from each proposal's projected 2D bounding box and supervise our 3D model to predict this embedding on a per-instance basis. Second, to enhance zero-shot capability and inject domain-specific information, we employ a powerful Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) as an image captioner to generate rich textual captions for each of these proposals. These captions are integrated into the training objective to directly align the 3D features with these rich semantics, creating a composite loss that combines direct feature distillation with caption-based semantic enrichment. Our experiments validate the effectiveness of our approach, establishing a new state of the art in 3D open-vocabulary detection on the Waymo Open Dataset and nuScenes.

papers.title: Bridging Learned Visual Perception and Symbolic Belief-Space Planning via Probabilistic Grounding
papers.summary: In partially observable settings, agents must act without full knowledge of the world state and rely on uncertain state-estimation pipelines. Obtaining grounded and verifiable symbolic plans under such uncertainty remains a key challenge. Recent work has integrated Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to bridge perception and symbolic reasoning, following two main paradigms. The first, VLM-as-planner, maps images directly to action sequences, and the second, VLM-as-grounder, grounds observations into symbolic predicates used as the initial state by off-the-shelf planners. Both approaches ignore uncertainty in the planning process, compromising robustness. We introduce a third paradigm, VLM-as-probabilistic-grounder, a novel approach that captures the uncertainty of VLM predicate groundings as a probability distribution over symbolic states. This enables planning in belief space and producing robust plans under uncertainty. Experiments in simulated household robot settings show improved robustness and task success over deterministic grounding, underscoring how our approach leverages foundation models for reliable planning under uncertainty.

papers.summary: Characterizing user engagement is essential for developing effective human-computer interaction (HCI) applications, particularly for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). papers.title: SparseHPS: A Unified Model for Human Pose and Shape across Depth Cameras and LiDARs
papers.summary: Recovering 3D human pose and shape from point clouds is central to motion capture, robotics and self-driving vehicles, because depth cameras and LiDARs sense a person directly in metric 3D and work under any lighting. papers.title: C-ARC: Continuous-Adaptive Range Clustering for Non-Repetitive LiDAR Sensors
papers.summary: Real-time LiDAR clustering identifies structures in point clouds, which is an essential prerequisite for many mobile robotics algorithms. Their Rhodonea-curve trajectories produce non-uniform point distributions, and the absence of a rotation cycle renders conventional scan line indexing inapplicable. papers.title: One Behavior, Out of Order: Deterministic Execution and Parallel Simulation of ROS 2 Applications
papers.summary: System-level simulation is widely used to validate robotic applications before hardware deployment. However, Robot Operating System 2 (ROS 2), a popular middleware for such applications, uses asynchronous publish-subscribe communication, which can make application behavior depend on scheduling and the platform. The behavior can then vary across runs and machines even with the same inputs. This nondeterminism makes faults hard to reproduce and tests unreliable. In this paper, we first give ROS 2 applications a lightweight coordination scheme in which every component, including event-driven ones, reads its inputs and writes its outputs at predefined time instants. By decoupling computation and communication, the scheme makes an application deterministic, that is, it always has one behavior for given inputs. Tests are thus repeatable, but for large applications they still take a long time. To speed up these tests, we then present an out-of-order parallel simulation algorithm. From the predefined read and write instants, it knows before the run which activations of components depend on which. It starts each activation as soon as those it depends on have finished. Finally, we implement the algorithm in a simulator that runs existing ROS 2 applications without any change to them or to ROS 2. We evaluate the simulator on industrial use cases and synthetic graphs. On the industrial use cases, it is up to 2.6 times faster than synchronous parallel simulation and needs an order of magnitude less memory for messages than asynchronous parallel simulation.

papers.title: GroundAnything: Reconciling Parallel Decoding with Precise Visual Grounding at Flash Speed
papers.summary: Autoregressive (AR) grounding models serialize spatial predictions, introducing sequential latency and imposing a causal order on output tokens. We view grounding as visual evidence extraction: objects, locations, and spatial relations are jointly constrained by the image and query, yet their dependencies do not imply an intrinsic left-to-right generation order. This distinction makes bidirectional diffusion a natural fit, allowing spatial hypotheses to emerge in parallel and be jointly refined through iterative denoising. We introduce GroundAnything, a 4B-parameter grounding foundation model that reconciles fast parallel decoding with precise localization through blockwise denoising. Training combines grounding pretraining from public datasets and dedicated data engines, direct AR-to-diffusion conversion with joint AR and diffusion objectives, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO-based reinforcement post-training. papers.title: Beyond the Sink Interpretation: Radial Attention in Flow-Based VLA Policies
papers.summary: Prior work calls the high attention on the first and last action tokens of a flow-based VLA policy a radial action sink, and uses these tokens to set the execution horizon. The corresponding BH-equations are derived explicitly for the rotating and free floating body. Further, the Hamel equations for nonholonomically constrained rigid bodies are discussed, and demonstrated for the inhomogenous ball rolling on a plane.

papers.summary: Autonomous robots can transform how we observe marine ecosystems, enabling vision-based focal follows (animal tracking) at scale, but close-range operation in reefs and other cluttered habitats remains difficult. papers.title: Infer3D: Inverse Generative Modeling Enables Robust 3D Reconstruction
papers.summary: Humans can understand the 3D structure of scenes even from highly unfamiliar or extreme viewpoints. papers.title: Communications-free Collective Intelligence Via Allocentric Belief
papers.summary: A team of skilled card players share no information amongst each other, and yet still are able to coordinate their play by watching the same players and reading the same tells. Autonomous systems have failed to exploit this logic, relying instead on explicit communication or complex state estimation schemes that can fail when it matters most. Without it, decentralized agents diverge in their world beliefs, and coordination collapses. Here we show that anchoring all agents to a single shared external actor, a common witness whose reactions encode team state, produces spontaneous, communication-free coordination. An allocentric belief network trained on witness behavior allows each agent to independently reconstruct full team state, keeping group beliefs consistent with no inter-agent exchange. Across five competitive environments allocentric belief alignment outperforms egocentric approaches in collective performance, and even scales to sixty-agent teams where standard methods fail. These results establish a new principle for collective intelligence: in the absence of communication, a shared gaze replaces a shared channel.

papers.title: Counterfactual World Models: JEPAs That Reason About "What If"
papers.summary: World models operate in a world they cannot fully observe. When a hidden disturbance, such as a current pushing a boat, changes the outcome of an action, a counterfactual question follows: what would have happened under a different action, subject to the same disturbance? Its answer separates bad decisions from bad luck. We prove that world models trained on factual transitions cannot answer it on their own, whatever their data or capacity. For many physical systems, the observed outcome and a simple property of the dynamics suffice: natura non facit saltus, nature makes no leaps. When actions and disturbances act as separate forces, their interaction is second-order in time, so the counterfactual outcome is, to first order, the observed outcome plus the difference between the world model's predictions under the alternative and factual actions. This yields a counterfactual world model with no counterfactual data, extra parameters, or retraining. For transitions of duration $h$, we prove an $O(h^2)$ bound on the counterfactual error relative to the disturbance variance, establish a matching minimax lower bound from unpaired factual data, and characterize failures at discontinuities, coordinate folds, and disturbances that scale the command. We validate these predictions from pixels with JEPA world models on frozen DINOv2 and masked autoencoder (MAE) encoders. On four rendered simulators, our approach improves counterfactual $R^2$ from $38$--$46\%$ to $86$--$96\%$ with the same world models; on a fifth, an underwater vehicle, it reaches $90$--$94\%$ with sixteen times more factual data. Four further frozen encoders, DINOv3, SigLIP~2, CLIP and EVA-02, give $81$--$95\%$ on the same simulators. In hindsight planning, it finds the action that would have reached the goal in $35$--$69\%$ of events, against $14$--$23\%$ for an oracle planner that knows the simulator but not the outcome.

papers.title: Feasibility Ceilings Before Learning: Sizing and Timing Bounds for Drone-Mesh Interception

papers.title: Emo-H2A: Driving a Facial Robot Directly from LLM Hidden States at Token Rate
papers.summary: Diverse, semantically synchronized, and low-latency facial expressions are essential for human-robot interaction. While large language models (LLMs) have endowed anthropomorphic robots with fluent speech, facial expression still struggles to follow the conversation. Motivated by this gap, we present Emo-H2A (hidden-to-actuation), a paradigm that drives a facial robot directly from LLM hidden states during autoregressive decoding. Without a separate emotion label, expression stays continuous and context-sensitive, and the face moves with the unfolding reply. We instantiate this paradigm as EmoManifold, a training-free method that extracts a valence-arousal-dominance (VAD) coordinate from each hidden state, projects it, and drives the face at token granularity. The readout is checked on six language models, and the same projection drives our 29-degree-of-freedom (DoF) facial robot. When driven by this projection, the face shifts its expression in the matching direction on 87.5% of within-reply valence transitions, whereas holding a single label for the whole reply leaves directional tracking near the 50% chance level, and first moves in 0.96s rather than waiting 10-26s for the reply to finish and a turn-level label to return.

papers.title: Scalable Iterative Multi-Agent Path Finding under Turn Constraints
papers.summary: Large-scale multi-mobile-robot systems require fast and reliable path planning under realistic motion constraints. Multi-Agent Path Finding with turn actions (MAPF$_T$) explicitly models orientation changes and turn-induced delays, but these constraints increase the computational burden of search-based methods. Priority-inheritance-based planning offers a highly scalable alternative, yet directly extending it to MAPF$_T$ is nontrivial because turn actions break the immediate node-vacation assumption underlying conventional priority inheritance. To address this challenge, this paper proposes PIBT$^*_T$, an efficient iterative solver for MAPF$_T$. PIBT$^*_T$ advances scalable multi-agent coordination by preserving the lightweight single-timestep planning mechanism of Priority Inheritance with Backtracking (PIBT), while introducing dedicated mechanisms to handle turn-induced dependencies, local deadlocks, livelock, and inefficient repeated pushing. Experiments on standard MAPF benchmarks show that PIBT$^*_T$ achieves high success rates and strong scalability, solving instances with up to 1000 agents within seconds. For realistic engineering environments, Action Dependency Graph (ADG)-based execution simulation and a flexible manufacturing system case study show that turn-aware planning better reflects robot execution and reduces actual makespan compared with classical MAPF planning. Experiments with TurtleBot4 robots further validate the practical feasibility of the proposed method.

papers.title: Estimation-Aware Reachability
papers.summary: Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability computes the states from which a system can be kept safe under worst-case disturbances, but it assumes the state is known exactly, whereas real robots act on noisy estimates whose uncertainty evolves with their motion. We extend Hamilton-Jacobi Reachability to the robot's belief, estimate and uncertainty, treating unexpected measurements as a bounded adversary and enlarging the unsafe set by the current uncertainty, so that certified states are safe with a prescribed probability. The formulation is compatible with existing solvers. In simulation, the resulting safety filters nearly eliminate the collisions of certaintyequivalent HJ and are less conservative than equally safe uncertainty-padding baselines. The implementation code is available at https://github.com/HimanshuPaudel/Estimation-Aware-Reachability

papers.title: Controllable Generative Trajectory Prediction via Weak Preference Alignment
papers.summary: Deep generative models such as conditional variational autoencoders (CVAEs) have shown great promise for predicting trajectories of surrounding agents in autonomous vehicle planning. State-of-the-art models have achieved remarkable accuracy in such prediction tasks. Besides accuracy, diversity is also crucial for safe planning because human behaviors are inherently uncertain and multimodal. However, existing methods generally lack a scheme to generate controllably diverse trajectories, which is arguably more useful than randomly diversified trajectories, to the end of safe planning. To address this, we propose PrefCVAE, an augmented CVAE framework that uses weakly labeled preference pairs to imbue latent variables with semantic attributes. Using average velocity as an example attribute, we demonstrate that PrefCVAE enables controllable, semantically meaningful predictions without degrading baseline accuracy. Our results show the effectiveness of preference supervision as a cost-effective way to enhance sampling-based generative models.

papers.title: NIF-VIO: Visual--Inertial Odometry Across Inertial and Non-Inertial Reference Frames
papers.summary: Conventional visual--inertial odometry (VIO) assumes that observations from cameras and an inertial measurement unit (IMU) are jointly consistent in an inertial reference frame. However, this assumption breaks down under non-inertial conditions. Inside accelerating or rotating carriers, visual observations of the interior reflect carrier-relative motion, while IMU measurements contain additional carrier-induced components, which can compromise conventional fusion. We therefore present NIF-VIO for localization relative to the local environment across inertial and non-inertial reference frames. It adapts visual--inertial fusion based on measurement consistency. As inertial conditions change, early constraint isolation is combined with local reoptimization to limit error propagation before inconsistency confirmation and repair the affected local geometry. Under non-inertial conditions, a compact model with temporally shared parameters is introduced to account for carrier motion while preserving inertial information that complements visual constraints. Experiments on public benchmarks and a self-collected dataset demonstrate that NIF-VIO achieves competitive performance under inertial conditions and improved localization accuracy and availability under non-inertial conditions.

papers.title: A Differentiable Composite Approximation Framework for Autonomous Underwater Vehicle Maneuvering Modeling from Sea-Trial Data
papers.summary: Field-based modeling from onboard measurements can produce autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) maneuvering models that reflect real operating characteristics. From an approximation perspective, conventional maneuvering models use predefined constraint polynomial bases, whereas data-driven models use data-adaptive bases. Motivated by this basis-function view, this paper presents a differentiable composite approximation formulation, in which the polynomial basis component and the data-adaptive basis component are treated as differentiable parts of a unified predictor and calibrated jointly. A gradient-based co-calibration method is developed for full-scale AUV maneuvering prediction, where a sensitivity-aware mechanism regulates bounded polynomial updates while the neural residual captures remaining nonlinear discrepancies under a shared prediction objective. To account for ocean-current effects in field data, a turning-motion-based current estimation and compensation procedure is incorporated to construct current-compensated learning targets for training and rollout. The framework is evaluated using sea-trial data collected from a 7-meter AUV under multiple maneuvering conditions. Results show that the proposed method improves recursive trajectory and velocity prediction compared with polynomial-only, neural-only, and frozen-prior hybrid baselines, demonstrating its applicability to field-data-based AUV maneuvering modeling.

papers.title: Recoverability, Not Invariance: Certified Safety for Robots at the Limits of Performance
papers.summary: Safety certification in robotics typically rests on forward invariance of the deployed controller, a property that demands high-fidelity models at the edge of the operating envelope, exactly where models are least reliable and robots perform best. As a result, many of the behaviors we most want robots to run, from learned policies to aggressive maneuvers at the limits of traction, cannot be certified at all. We introduce recoverability, a contraction-theoretic safety concept that resolves this tension by certifying a robot's ability to reengage a trusted recovery mode rather than the invariance of a deployed behavior. We prove that switching to the recovery mode from anywhere inside a certified tube guarantees exponential convergence, even under disturbances and model error. To decide when to switch, we derive the contraction insertion gradient, the first-order effect of a recovery insertion on the certificate, and embed it in a switching-time program in which feasibility alone guarantees safety and optimality only shapes performance. To supply the certificates, we develop sequential convex synthesis that monotonically grows the certified tube toward the exact viability kernel. We validate our approach in simulated quadrotor flight through uncertain obstacles, where it outperforms invariance-based safety filters, and in hardware deployments aboard a full-scale IndyNXT autonomous racecar, where it repeatedly recovers the car from an aggressive raceline at the limits of handling in the rain. Recoverability provides a certified exit strategy, extending formal safety guarantees to aggressive, learned, and experimental behaviors without requiring their invariance.

papers.title: DOCK: Dual-Stream-Inspired Self-Supervised Object-Centric Representations Grounded in Robot Kinematics
papers.summary: Latent-space planners select actions by comparing the embedding of a predicted future image with that of a goal image. This assumes that distance in the embedding reflects how far the scene is from the goal. We profile this assumption with simulator-executed futures, which removes prediction error. For six frozen DINO and V-JEPA encoders, feature distance barely tracks the object's distance to its goal: the rank correlation is at most 0.11, against 0.87 for object-mask centroids. It is dominated by background and robot patches, and frozen-feature readouts capture the arm far better than the object. Inspired by the ventral (what) and dorsal (where/how) visual streams, we propose DOCK, which learns an object representation whose changes agree with measured physical motion. A grasped object moves with the gripper, so forward kinematics on the joint angles gives a proxy for the object's displacement without annotation. From 9,951 held-object transport trajectories in 21 simulated kitchen scenes, we mine 404K displacement pairs and train three components: an object token pooled from patch features (what), a spatial ruler that makes differences of readout coordinates equal to measured displacements (where), and a dynamics predictor over object tokens (how). Used as a planning cost, the learned representation places the object in 15 of 21 tasks, as many as an oracle that reads the true object position, while mask geometry reaches 10 and frozen feature distance 9. It still solves the most tasks when the unseen robot arm is visible, and its ranking transfers to held-out layouts with unseen object instances and categories without any adaptation.

papers.title: Reducing the Power Required for Multi-UAV Tethered Payload Transportation via a Rotating Equilibrium
papers.summary: Collaborative aerial transportation of tethered payloads is fundamentally limited by space, power, and weight constraints. Conventional approaches rely on static equilibrium conditions, where each vehicle tilts to generate the forces that ensure they maintain a formation geometry that avoids aerodynamic interactions and collision. This horizontal thrust component represents a significant energy penalty compared to the ideal case in which each vehicle produces purely vertical thrust to lift the payload. Operating in tighter tether configurations can minimize this effect, but at the cost of either having to fly the vehicles in closer proximity, which risks collision, or significantly increasing the length of the tether, which increases complexity and reduces potential use-cases. We propose operating the tether-suspended flying system at a rotating equilibrium. By maintaining steady circular motion, centrifugal forces provide the necessary horizontal tether tension, allowing each quadrotor to generate purely vertical thrust and thus reducing the total force (and power) required compared to an equilibrium where the thrusts are not vertical. It also allows for a wider range of tether configurations to be used without sacrificing efficiency. Results demonstrate that rotating equilibria can reduce power consumption relative to static lifting by up to 20%, making collaborative aerial solutions more practically relevant.

papers.title: Hebbian self-organization of monosynaptic reflexes in a biologically realistic multiarticular limb
papers.summary: Spinal monosynaptic reflexes depend on patterns of connectivity between muscle spindle afferents and motoneurons that should reflect musculoskeletal dynamics. One possibility is that the details of these circuits are specified genetically, but this requires an unlikely coevolution of musculoskeletal and neural elements. Here we show how biomechanical structure can determine the connectivity of self-organized spinal circuits. Using a neuromechanical model combining a multi-joint limb, proprioceptive feedback, and Hebbian plasticity driven by motor babbling, we find that biologically realistic connectivity emerges spontaneously when babbling is neither too sparse nor too frequent. This results in strong homonymous projections, weaker heteronymous projections among functional synergists, and very weak connections among antagonists. This outcome also depends on musculoskeletal morphometry. Heteronymous synergies form when proximal muscles are strongest---the characteristic gradient of mammalian limbs--whereas excessively strong biarticular muscles lead to unphysiological antagonist coupling. The mechanisms differ: homonymous connections arise from direct sensorimotor correlation during fusimotor coactivation by beta motoneurons, while heteronymous connections depend on multi-joint dynamics that emerge only after homonymous reflexes stabilize and increasing muscle strength generates multisegmental motion. Overall, this study provides a mechanistic basis for fetal sensorimotor development and generates testable predictions about the consequences of naturally occurring and experimentally induced variations.

papers.title: Learned versus Kinematic Trajectory Prediction under Reduced Observation Frequency
papers.summary: Trajectory prediction models for automated driving are usually trained on data with a fixed sampling frequency, while positions received via vehicle-to-everything (V2X) communication arrive at 1-10 Hz. We study whether a learned predictor that uses only the observation history keeps its advantage over constant velocity (CV) and constant acceleration (CA) models when the history frequency drops. On the Argoverse 2 motion forecasting dataset, the 5 s history of the focal agent was downsampled from 10 Hz to 5, 2, and 1 Hz, and the 6 s future was predicted without maps or neighboring agents. An LSTM-based recurrent neural network (RNN) trained for each frequency was compared with the same network trained at 10 Hz and applied to sparse histories after linear interpolation. Hypotheses and thresholds were fixed before training, the main RNNs were trained with ten seeds each, and results on 24,984 test scenarios have bootstrap confidence intervals over scenarios and seeds. The average displacement error of the frequency-specific RNN grew by 3.1% at 5 Hz, 10.1% at 2 Hz, and 20.3% at 1 Hz. Contrary to our hypothesis, its advantage over the better kinematic model did not vanish on straight motion and was 24-30% on both straight motion and turns at every frequency, while for pedestrians CV was more accurate. The 10 Hz model with interpolation was at most 1.3% less accurate than the frequency-specific model down to 2 Hz but 11.5% less accurate at 1 Hz. Each hypothesis was only partly supported.

papers.title: WoRD: Diffusion-Based Posterior Inference for Online Goal Recognition
papers.summary: Goal recognition is the task of inferring an agent's intended goal from its observed behavior. Most existing work focuses on high-level symbolic recognition, abstracting away the continuous motion through which agents reach their goal. Methods that do reason over continuous trajectories rely on an explicit dynamics model that is hard to acquire and rarely transfers across settings. Neither approach explicitly learns how agents move toward each candidate goal, limiting accuracy on ambiguous trajectory prefixes where such knowledge is most needed. We present WoRD (Waypoint Recognition with Diffusion), which uses a learned trajectory prior to infer the agent's goal from partial observations. At each step, WoRD runs one warm-started denoising chain per candidate goal, steers each chain toward the observed trajectory through a closed-form log-likelihood gradient, and reweights the resulting samples by Bayes' rule into a calibrated posterior over goals. We evaluate WoRD on simulated robot settings, pedestrian trajectories, and vehicle trajectories using four metrics targeting distinct failure modes. Across all three settings, the same inference procedure preserves calibrated multimodal beliefs through ambiguous prefixes where filter- and classifier-based observers collapse to a single mode or grow overconfident.

papers.title: Capability Composition in Heterogeneous Teams via Barrier-Guided Diffusion Sampling
papers.summary: The agents in a heterogeneous team can cooperate to accomplish tasks that exceed their individual capabilities. The team trajectories for a cooperative task can be generated by a generative model, provided that the model has been trained on demonstrations of the agents cooperating. Yet, demonstrations of cooperation are costly and may not exist for tasks that the team has never performed. The conditions under which the agents can combine their capabilities, however, are physical properties of the team and are known before any demonstration is collected. We encode the conditions as constraints on the team trajectories, and we enforce the constraints while sampling from generative models trained on demonstrations of each agent alone. We prove that the proposed method can generate every team trajectory that satisfies the constraints, although the demonstrations contain no cooperation. Hence the constraints determine which team trajectories can be generated, and the demonstrations determine how likely each team trajectory is. Numerical results on two cooperative tasks show the effectiveness of the method, which generates cooperative team trajectories that satisfy the constraints and requires no retraining when agents join or leave the team. Finally, we implement the method on a multi-robot testbed.

papers.title: Supervised Learning Approaches for Static and Temporal Force Prediction in a Biohybrid Muscle Ring Actuator
papers.summary: Skeletal muscle-based biohybrid actuators have proved to be a promising component in soft robotics, offering efficient movement. However, their intrinsic biological variability and nonlinearity pose significant challenges for controllability and predictability. To address these issues, this study investigates the application of supervised learning, a form of machine learning, to model and predict the behavior of biohybrid machines (BHMs), focusing on a muscle ring anchored on flexible polymer pillars. First, static prediction models (i.e., random forest and neural network regressors) are trained to estimate the maximum exerted force achieved from input variables such as muscle sample, electrical stimulation parameters, and baseline exerted force. Second, a dynamic modeling framework, based on Long Short-Term Memory networks, is developed to replicate the time series of exerted forces observed. Both modeling approaches demonstrate high predictive accuracy. The best performance of the static models is characterized by a mean R2 of 0.9346, whereas the dynamic model achieves a mean R2 of 0.9944 over five training instances. The static models can enable optimization of muscle actuator performance for targeted applications and required force outcomes, while the dynamic model provides a foundation for developing robustly adaptive control strategies in future biohybrid robotic systems.

papers.title: Magflow: Differentiable Simulation of Industrial-Grade 6D Magnetic Levitation
papers.summary: Magnetic levitation with six-degrees-of-freedom enables frictionless transport and micrometer-scale positioning in principle, but low-level control is inherently challenging due to its complex and unstable dynamics. Industrial systems typically rely on deep hardware-software co-design, where mover and stator geometries are jointly designed to enable a compact, hand-crafted approximation of the electromagnetic force computation, thereby keeping control computationally tractable at kilohertz rates. However, this approach imposes overly conservative constraints on the operating workspace and the range of supported mover topologies. Instead of reducing the underlying physics to a hand-crafted approximation, we compute the physics directly. We introduce Magflow, a fully differentiable, GPU-parallel simulator for 6D magnetic levitation. It is used to train the first neural controller for an industrial-grade 6D magnetic levitation system that is learned purely from simulated physics. We show that the learned neural controller transfers zero-shot from simulation to real hardware while satisfying hard real-time constraints at 4 kHz. The learned controller achieves qualitatively new behaviors and even levitates a mover topology for which no hand-crafted solution exists. These results demonstrate that co-design is not a physical necessity for 6D magnetic levitation control. More broadly, control learning from simulated physics can find solutions beyond the reach of control engineering in demanding industrial domains. Source code and demonstration videos are publicly available at https://sites.google.com/view/magflow.

papers.title: Adapting Generalist Vehicle Models for High-Speed MPC Across Terrains
papers.summary: High-speed off-road autonomy requires precise closed-loop control for a target vehicle while remaining robust across changing terrains. Recent forward kinodynamic (FKD) prediction foundation models suggest a promising path, starting from a generalist model and specializing it to the target platform. OptCar introduces a transformer FKD architecture that uses FiLM to condition multi-step predictions on a single dynamics context token summarizing recent state-action history. It then specializes the generalist model using limited real-world data and targeted synthetic rollouts from environment-specific system identification. In closed-loop model predictive control (MPC) experiments across three terrains and an out-of-distribution cart-pulling task, the largest gains appear at 6 m/s, the highest speed evaluated and the regime in which slip dominates tracking error. On vegetation + dirt, the most slip-diverse terrain, OptCar reduces 6 m/s trajectory tracking error by roughly 55% relative to AnyCar fine-tuned on real data alone, and remains the most accurate even when an unseen cart payload changes the dynamics. papers.title: Arboreus: A Realistic Boreal Forest Simulator with Topographic Terrain and Satellite-Informed Parametric Tree Distributions
papers.summary: This work presents Arboreus, a realistic Boreal forest simulator, developed to support statistical validation of robotic autonomy algorithms in Boreal forest environments. Arboreus presents an automated methodology for synthesizing large-scale, data-informed, plausible forest worlds from parametric trees, height-variant terrain, and satellite-informed tree density distributions. The parametric generation of dominant Boreal tree species such as Birch, Spruce, and Pine is guided by trunk, canopy, and foliage parameters, extracted from growth studies in the Nordic areas. Tree distribution in an area of interest is guided by the Copernicus satellite dataset, which provides tree cover density and dominant species type at up to 10m raster resolution. The forest floor generation is guided by topographic data from the Swedish cadastral agency to produce realistic data-informed terrains. Given coordinates and extents of forested areas of interest, Arboreus synthesizes data-informed plausible forests, while offering flexibility to inject user observations of real forests (detail, age, dimensionality and tree count), which is critical for realistic synthetic data generation and for the testing of feature-sensitive autonomy algorithms. The applicability of Arboreus for benchmarking and validation of robot autonomy for different robot mobilities is demonstrated in Gazebosim, Unreal Engine, and Isaac Sim physics engines. The applicability of Arboreus as a source of synthetic forest data and its potential to support downstream forest resource mapping research (volume estimation, tree instance segmentation and stem attribute estimation) is also demonstrated. papers.title: GroundingPI: A Grounding Foundation Model towards Physical Intelligence with Visual Primitives
papers.summary: Precise grounding matters. It specifies which object is the target and where that object is, even in clutter and for tiny objects, and it has to be fast enough for closed-loop control. Yet vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) take perception from general-purpose vision-language and video-generation backbones, which still fail in these settings. We introduce GroundingPI, a 4B grounding foundation model that generates points and boxes as quantized coordinates in a shared vocabulary. Training combines multimodal and spatial pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning with GRPO, using supervision from public datasets and dedicated data engines. Against 44 baselines across 34 grounding benchmarks spanning 11 perceptual capabilities, GroundingPI establishes a new state of the art, averaging 73.68%, above the larger GPT-6 Astra (71.54%). As a downstream visual backbone, GroundingPI improves performance on robotic manipulation and autonomous driving. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboCasa-GR1, it outperforms all evaluated backbones in all four out-of-distribution settings, with relative gains of up to 24.8% over the strongest baseline. On RoboCasa-GR1, GroundingPI trained with 50% of the demonstrations outperforms those baselines trained with 75%. Its mean open-loop L2 error on nuScenes is 0.296 m. We systematically analyze GroundingPI's pretraining in scale and data composition. Grounding quality and downstream manipulation improve with pretraining scale, with generalization tracking perceptual gains most closely. Analyzing the data recipe across these 11 perceptual capabilities shows dense grounding's substantial benefits for both, and OCR's potential as a catalyst for perceptual learning. These results support grounding as a perceptual foundation, and dedicated perceptual pretraining as a promising direction for foundation models of physical intelligence.

papers.title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
papers.summary: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.

papers.title: AgentMoT: An Agentic Mixture-of-Transformers for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
papers.summary: Driving models need to choose which capabilities to use and when to reconsider their decisions. We introduce AgentMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers with built-in agent reasoning and system scheduling. Combinations of agent, world, and action experts form three jointly trained pathways for direct-action, vision-language-action, and world-action computation. The Router selects a native pathway, while the agent expert supplies reasoning and selects skills. Execution feedback raises wake-up requests, and the agent self-scheduler learns whether to reconsider the task decision or keep it. Mandatory requests invoke the agent directly. papers.title: ReactBench-AD: Do Driving VLAs and World-Action Models React to Imminent Hazards in Their Path?
papers.summary: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) and World-Action Models (WAMs) have emerged in autonomous driving with the promise of strong generalization to long-tail scenarios. papers.title: Pruning Autonomous Driving VLAs: What to Preserve for Reasoning and Action

papers.title: Composable Driving Style for End-to-End Autonomous Driving

papers.title: PhyMotion: Structured 3D Motion Reward for Physics-Grounded Human Video Generation
papers.summary: Generating realistic human motion is a central yet unsolved challenge in video generation. While reinforcement learning (RL)-based post-training has driven recent gains in general video quality, extending it to human motion remains bottlenecked by a reward signal that cannot reliably score motion realism. Existing video rewards primarily rely on 2D perceptual signals, without explicitly modeling the 3D body state, contact, and dynamics underlying articulated human motion, and often assign high scores to videos with floating bodies or physically implausible movements. To address this, we propose PhyMotion, a structured, fine-grained motion reward that grounds recovered 3D human trajectories in a physics simulator and evaluates motion quality along multiple dimensions of physical feasibility. Concretely, we recover SMPL body meshes from generated videos, retarget them onto a humanoid in the MuJoCo physics simulator, and evaluate the resulting motion along three axes: kinematic plausibility, contact and balance consistency, and dynamic feasibility. Each component provides a continuous and interpretable signal tied to a specific aspect of motion quality, allowing the reward to capture which aspects of motion are physically correct or violated. Experiments show that PhyMotion achieves stronger correlation with human judgments than existing reward formulations. These gains carry over to RL-based post-training, where optimizing PhyMotion leads to larger and more consistent improvements than optimizing existing rewards, improving motion realism across both autoregressive and bidirectional video generators under both automatic metrics and blind human evaluation (+68 Elo gain). Ablations show that the three axes provide complementary supervision signals, while the reward preserves overall video generation quality with only modest training overhead.

papers.title: LLM Persuasion Is in the Eye of the Evaluation
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have already been shown to match or exceed human experts in persuasion. While their persuasive capabilities hold promise for beneficial uses such as education and health communication, they can also be used to manipulate and misinform, making their evaluation a growing priority for developers and regulators. That evaluation, however, remains fragmented: studies differ in what they treat as persuasion, and broad claims often rest on narrow, situation-specific assessments. Automated methods, often modelled on human studies, offer a way to compare such assessments directly, as they can be run on the same models at scale and can include high-risk forms of persuasion that would be difficult or unethical to test on people. In this study, we adapt nine published automated methods to a shared setup, run them on the same fifteen LLMs, and ask whether their rankings agree and why. We find that the methods agree only weakly (mean Spearman $ρ= 0.25$). Our analyses point to two contributing factors. Models that refuse some tasks but not others, directly or indirectly, lower agreement by about a quarter, and these refusals fall mostly on manipulation tasks. General capability also plays a part: most rational persuasion (non-manipulative) methods track it, whereas most manipulation methods do not. Together, these findings suggest that agreement depends more on the task a method sets than on how it scores persuasion, although this pattern is only indicative given the eight methods available for analysis. More broadly, our results suggest that persuasion scores combine a model's ability to persuade with its willingness to do so. A single score is therefore informative about its own setting, but says little about a model's persuasiveness across tasks.

papers.title: Learning What to Change: State-Verified Reinforcement Learning for Educational Agents
papers.summary: Persistent tutoring agents do more than answer questions: they manage course files, practice records, and learner profiles that govern future lessons. papers.title: Reward Blindness: A Theoretical Framework for Diagnosing Reinforcement Learning Reward Limitations in Text-to-SQL

papers.title: On Adaptive Step Sizes for Eligibility Traces in Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Many deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms store agent-environment interactions in a replay buffer and later learn by sampling transitions from it. However, this approach can be memory-inefficient and can delay learning because the agent can learn from a transition only when the buffer samples it. Additionally, most of these methods use one-step or short multi-step temporal-difference (TD) updates, which are slow at credit assignment. An alternative approach is to learn from the stream of observations as they arrive without relying on a buffer. Eligibility-trace algorithms allow these incremental updates and can also assign credit over many steps. These algorithms were common with linear function approximation but have only recently been used in deep RL. Basic questions, such as how to use vector step sizes with eligibility traces in the deep RL setting, remain open. In this work, we first show that adaptive vector step sizes must be part of the eligibility trace to keep the equivalence between the forward and backward views. We then show that the step sizes of common optimizers, such as Adam, do not have an online backward view. We introduce a new optimizer, Function-Space Distance (FSD), that maintains the forward-backward equivalence. We test four eligibility-trace algorithms covering semi-gradient and gradient TD updates, as well as value-based and actor-critic methods. We show that FSD performs better than SGD or naively applied Adam. The resulting algorithms outperform or match other streaming methods and are comparable to or better than PPO, which uses a buffer, in most environments. papers.title: Broad-Persistent Advising in Interactive Reinforcement Learning via Latent State Encoding
papers.summary: Deep Interactive Reinforcement Learning (Deep IntRL) accelerates reinforcement learning training by incorporating external advice. However, conventional Deep IntRL uses each piece of advice only in the current step and discards it after a single interaction. Persistent Advising and Broad-Persistent Advising (BPA) extend this process by storing advice in persistent memory and reusing it in similar states through state generalisation based on K-means clustering. This research proposes Encoder BPA, which employs a latent encoder to retrieve and reuse advice. In this framework, a trained encoder is used to map a state sequence into a latent representation at every time step. Advice can be retrieved through latent comparison, together with a top-(k) aggregation and a consistency condition to improve reuse stability. Experimental results show that Encoder BPA improves learning efficiency and advice utilisation at an early stage of training compared with different Deep IntRL approaches, especially in complex and partially observable environments.

papers.title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain
papers.summary: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.

papers.title: The Stability Gap in Continual Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Continual reinforcement learning (CRL) aims to enable agents to adapt to changing tasks while preserving previously acquired capabilities. Evaluation often relies on final aggregate metrics that can hide temporary performance degradation during adaptation. This work introduces a simple CRL benchmark that varies observation representations while preserving environment dynamics and rewards, supporting proof-of-concept demonstrations, inexpensive experimentation, and easily reproducible sanity checks. Using this benchmark, we demonstrate the stability gap in CRL: a substantial drop in prior-task performance after the introduction of new tasks, followed by partial or complete recovery. This pattern occurs despite the agent having complete access to past tasks.

papers.title: Noise Steering: Exploiting Wake Steering and Acoustic Directivity for Noise-Constrained Wind Farm Control via Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: Existing noise mitigation strategies for wind farms usually consist in reducing turbines power output, without accounting for the wake interactions between them and the noise emission directivity. This leads to over-conservative policies and unexploited wind power. Yet, turbine yaw can simultaneously affect wake interactions and the direction of noise emission, offering an additional degree of freedom for farm-level noise control. We therefore propose Noise Steering, a model-free reinforcement learning (RL) strategy that jointly controls turbine yaw angles and power setpoints to maximise farm power while satisfying a local noise constraint in a defined region. To enable training at a reduced computational cost, a low-fidelity acoustic model is coupled with the steady-state FLORIS simulator. The RL agent effectively learns how to redirect wakes and noise directivity away from the protected region while redistributing power across the farm. On a six-turbine test farm, the policy satisfies the 40 dB noise constraint throughout the full range of turbulent winds, with an average power deficit of only 2% relative to greedy unimpeded control, and up to 7.7% at high wind speeds. In comparison, the industry-standard noise-reduced operation (NRO) baseline here generates an average power loss of 17%. When deployed in the higher-fidelity FASTFarm simulator, the policy largely retains its performance under steady and turbulent inflow, despite differences in simulation fidelity. These results demonstrate the potential of combining yaw control and power derating through RL to improve the power-noise trade-off in wind farm operation.

papers.title: SiliconGym: A Versatile Reinforcement Learning Environment for Agentic EDA

papers.title: Decision-Focused Reinforcement Learning for LLM Post-Training
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promise as predictors across various tasks, benefiting from their ability to use information from unstructured context. However, when predictions serve as parameters of downstream optimization problems, higher prediction accuracy does not necessarily translate into lower decision costs. We propose decision-focused reinforcement learning (DFRL), a framework for post-training LLMs to predict optimization parameters using negative downstream decision regret as reward. DFRL trains LLM predictors to minimize the costs of the decisions induced by their predictions, without requiring downstream convexity or differentiability, and integrates readily into existing RL post-training frameworks. To address expensive reward evaluation, we develop two approaches. Heuristic warm-starting uses inexpensive approximate rewards during an initial phase before switching to refinement with exact rewards. Reward correction combines inexpensive estimates with randomized exact evaluations, preserving the expected policy gradient while reducing the expected number of exact solves per update. Experiments on three synthetic optimization problems demonstrate improvements over prediction-loss baselines, while a larger knapsack experiment shows faster early improvement under short training budgets. On inventory planning with H&M transactions and product descriptions, our best configuration, in which the LLM reasons before predicting, reduces regret by 31.4% relative to the SFT baseline and 12.4% relative to the strongest evaluated conventional forecasting baseline.

papers.title: JUDOR: CTDE-Based Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for the Co-Optimization of Joint UAV Motion and Decentralized Opportunistic Routing in Delay-Tolerant Network
papers.summary: The growing deployment of delay-tolerant networks (DTNs) has made store-carry-forward (SCF) communication indispensable for operating under sparse intermittent connectivity. However, intermittent contact opportunities, finite node buffers, and limited message time-to-live (TTL) degrade message delivery performance and induce network congestion. Yet unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), with extended radio coverage and controllable trajectories, can bridge ground-node pairs that would otherwise suffer poor connectivity. Nevertheless, conventional routing schemes decouple UAV motion control from message replication, and consequently fail to leverage UAV mobility to proactively create future contact opportunities. This paper presents JUDOR (Joint-UAV-Decentralized-Opportunistic-Routing), a centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE)-based multi-agent reinforcement learning framework optimized for joint discrete UAV heading control and decentralized opportunistic routing. Specifically, we model the tightly coupled UAV motion-routing co-optimization task as a factored partially observable Markov decision process with a shared team reward. JUDOR adopts decentralized actors for local-node execution and a centralized critic used exclusively in training, with optional multi-horizon congestion-hotspot auxiliary supervision. Through evaluation across four distinct traffic modes, JUDOR yields consistent performance gains over both classical and learning-based DTN baselines, including PRoPHET and MaxProp, whilst preserving contact-limited decentralized execution suitable for real-world DTN deployments.

papers.title: Design Optimization of Nuclear Fusion Reactor through Deep Reinforcement Learning
papers.summary: In this research, we investigate deep reinforcement learning (DRL) as a practical tool for constrained, multi-objective optimization for tokamak fusion reactor designs. The task is to optimize the design configurations that minimize building cost while achieving high energy gain and long energy confinement time, subject to the four operational limits required for stable operation. Due to the coupled physics-engineering evaluation, the resulting objectives and constraints are black-box, making it challenging to find optimal solutions with conventional search strategies. To address this, we implement Reward-Constrained Policy Optimization (RCPO) for tokamak fusion reactor design. This method integrates multiple constraints into the reward functions, guiding the policy towards feasible solutions and simplifying the design optimization process. Our numerical results show that the proposed DRL-based approach finds more feasible designs that satisfy operational constraints more efficiently than other data-driven optimization methods, demonstrating the potential of DRL for efficient future reactor design.

papers.title: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Heat Pump and Underfloor Heating Control: An End-to-End Case Study
papers.summary: Efficient control of underfloor heating (UFH) systems coupled with heat pumps (HPs) is challenging due to the high thermal inertia of buildings and the slow dynamic response of UFH systems. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) offers a data-driven control approach capable of simultaneously optimizing energy consumption and thermal comfort. However, the application of DRL-based controllers in occupied buildings under real operating conditions remains limited. This work presents and end-to-end case study (development, evaluation, and real-world deployment) of a DRL-based controller for an integrated UFH-HP system. First, a simulation-based pilot study was conducted to assess different DRL algorithms, control strategies, and configurations. Subsequently, a digital twin of a real residential building was developed and used to train DRL agents under simulated operating conditions. The best-performing agent was then deployed in the physical building without additional online fine-tuning. The results show that the controller successfully maintained indoor temperatures within the prescribed comfort limits while dynamically adjusting the HP supply temperature and UFH valve positions. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of deploying DRL controllers in occupied buildings and highlight their robustness and the practical challenges associated with transferring control policies from digital environments to real heating systems.

papers.title: ArgGYM: A Procedural, Engine-Verified Benchmark for Structured Defeasible Reasoning
papers.summary: Recent progress in large language model reasoning has been driven by benchmarks and reinforcement learning environments with automatically verifiable rewards, particularly in mathematics, code, and formal logic. These settings make model accuracy easier to evaluate and optimize, but it remains unclear how far success under fixed problem specifications and stable evaluation criteria transfers to reasoning outside such domains. Real-world reasoning often proceeds under incomplete and revisable information: conclusions may be supported provisionally, defeated by counter-evidence, reinstated by further arguments, or revised when stronger reasons become available. Reasoning of this kind is generally referred to as defeasible reasoning. We introduce ArgGYM, a procedural benchmark and RLVR-compatible training environment for structured defeasible reasoning. ArgGYM decomposes this reasoning into twelve tasks and grounds task-specific scoring in a symbolic argumentation engine that computes the formal states used to evaluate model outputs. It includes a frozen benchmark of 1,440 verified instances across fifteen curriculum configurations, two argument preference orderings, and two set orderings, while the same generators and verifiers can produce fresh instances, reducing dependence on static test sets, for both evaluation and verifiable-reward training. On the frozen benchmark, frontier and open-weight models show sharply different reasoning profiles: they can recover substantial parts of structured answers without solving the complete task, and performance declines in later curriculum configurations with longer dependencies and more interacting structures. Training Qwen3.5-4B with ArgGYM's verifiers as rewards more than doubles complete-task success on held-out instances, with the largest gains on constructive tasks.

papers.title: Beyond the Leaderboard: A Synthesis of Tool-Use, Planning, and Reasoning Failures in Large Language Model Agents
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly evaluated on their ability to use tools, plan multi-step tasks, coordinate with other agents, and operate over extended horizons. Reported benchmark gains often obscure recurring failure modes documented across otherwise unrelated evaluation efforts. This paper synthesizes 27 benchmark, taxonomy, and audit papers (2023-2026), spanning 19 distinct benchmarks, into a cross-cutting taxonomy of agent limitations. To our knowledge, this is the first synthesis that integrates evidence across tool use, planning, long-horizon reasoning, multi-agent coordination, safety, and measurement validity into a single, unified taxonomy of LLM agent limitations. We identify six failure clusters: (1) tool invocation and parameter-level errors, (2) planning and constraint-satisfaction failures, (3) long-horizon degradation from context accumulation, (4) multi-agent coordination failures, (5) safety and security failures under adversarial or underspecified conditions, and (6) measurement validity problems. The taxonomy was derived iteratively by grouping independently reported error categories into themes corresponding to distinct stages of the agent reasoning-to-action pipeline. Across the literature, we find that failures compound nonlinearly with task length, that strong performance on individual sub-tasks does not reliably translate into end-to-end success, and that additional scaffolding does not consistently improve reliability. At the same time, substantial progress has been demonstrated in single-turn tool use, short-horizon web navigation, and narrowly scoped coding tasks.
