papers.title: Spherical Boltzmann machines: a solvable theory of learning and generation in energy-based models
papers.summary: Energy-based models (EBMs) are flexible generative architectures inspired by statistical physics, but their learning and generative properties remain poorly understood. Here, we analyze a solvable EBM in the high-dimensional limit: the spherical Boltzmann machine (SBM). Combining tools from random matrix theory and dynamical mean-field theory, we: derive and solve closed equations describing the training dynamics of the SBM in the high-dimensional limit; compute the asymptotic Bayesian evidence, which acts as a partition function in parameter space and encodes global properties of the trained model; and uncover cascades of phase transitions that occur both during training and as a function of hyperparameters, related to successive alignment and condensation of the top modes of the coupling matrix to the data. We connect these transitions to sampling-time generative phenomena in a teacher-student scenario, including: sampling temperature tuning, double descent as a function of regularization strength, tempered posterior effects, and out-of-equilibrium effects during training that induce biases in the trained model. We provide numerical evidence showing that all these phenomena appear in standard generative architectures, beyond the SBM.

papers.title: Auditing Learned Dynamics in Weather Models
papers.summary: Learned weather models are experimentally accessible computational systems whose internal representations can be inspected and manipulated. Using sparse autoencoder features from GraphCast, DeepMind's autoregressive weather forecasting model, we test whether causal relevance requires physical semantics, a question that matters for auditing whether AI forecasters used in high-assurance settings rely on reliable mechanisms. We also look at whether physically associated latent directions can be steered to improve extreme-event forecasts, where interventions are applied to the model's internal activations during the rollout. We find that ablating a feature locked to GraphCast's computational mesh increases global geopotential height error despite lacking conventional physical semantics. Second, suppressing convection- and low-level-vorticity-associated features weakens predicted tropical-cyclone deepening (the fall in central pressure during intensification), while amplifying them reduces intensity error, with amplification of convection features through feature scaling achieving a median of 51\% error reduction over seven storms. Together, these results separate interpretable, physical association from causal utility and establish sparse features as experimental coordinates for auditing and intervening on learned weather dynamics.

papers.title: Virasoro Symmetry in Neural Network Field Theories
papers.summary: We construct the Virasoro algebra from a neural free-field architecture. A logarithmic momentum law and a smooth spectral window give the weight-one current kernel, whose radial-ordering discontinuity fixes the oscillator pairing. The limiting neural current correlations agree with the Fock vacuum correlations. Their Sugawara stress tensor gives the Virasoro algebra with central charge one, and charged vertex insertions identify its highest-weight sectors. Bounds on regulator and feature errors control finite-mode approximations to this representation. At finite width, an explicit adjoint-compatible projection defines an auxiliary Fock readout when its Hermitian mixed block is positive. Cauchy features extend the construction to fermionic and supersymmetric sectors, including a Clifford zero mode in the Ramond representation, while first-order stress tensors give fermionic and bosonic ghost systems. Shared reflected features impose scalar boundary conditions in every realization and yield conformal and superconformal gluing in the limiting fields. Numerical comparisons support the current pairing and field correlations; their detailed analysis is collected in the appendices.

papers.title: Hierarchical Pooling for Sheaf Neural Networks
papers.summary: Sheaf neural networks (SNNs) extend graph neural networks by operating on cellular sheaves, which assign to each node and edge its own vector space, along with linear restriction maps from node spaces to the spaces associated with their incident edges. These maps determine the sheaf Laplacian and can be learned at each layer, enabling layer-specific diffusion dynamics. Existing SNN architectures, however, always diffuse on the same graph, with restriction maps that may change across layers but continue to act on the original nodes and edges. We introduce Hierarchical Sheaf Pooling (HiSP), a pooling layer that enables hierarchical representation learning in SNNs. Following the Select-Reduce-Connect-Lift framework, HiSP groups fine-scale nodes, reduces their features using the fine-scale sheaf structure, and constructs the corresponding coarse graph. A new sheaf is then learned at the coarse resolution. By interleaving sheaf diffusion and pooling, HiSP enables hierarchical SNNs to learn distinct diffusion dynamics across layers and graph resolutions. This construction supports multiscale problems in which aggregation changes both the interacting entities and their relations.

papers.title: Does AI Assistance Preserve or Collapse Disagreement? A Study of Pre-Annotations in Ambiguous Video Labeling
papers.summary: AI-generated Pre-Annotations can accelerate video labeling, but they may also anchor annotators to model priors and suppress disagreement that is valuable for pluralistic dataset construction. We study this tradeoff in ambiguous temporal video annotation, where annotators choose event boundaries and assign context-dependent labels such as "normal" or "abnormal." We introduce a controlled audit protocol that separates annotation cost, consensus alignment, inter-annotator consistency, temporal-boundary variation, semantic-label variation, latent-space standardization, and edit behavior. In a counterbalanced pilot study with 18 annotators and 180 annotation sessions, a fixed CLIP-based Pre-Annotation engine reduced mean annotation time by 23.11%; 72% of annotators were faster with assistance, with a median per-annotator gain of 35%. Assistance increased inter-annotator consistency and CLIP-space standardization, while semantic-label entropy changed only slightly in aggregate. A six-annotator human consensus diagnostic showed comparable alignment across conditions (AMI $\approx 0.64$ in both conditions), but this diagnostic is self-including and should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as independent evidence that model influence is absent. Overall, the results suggest that Pre-Annotations acted mainly as editable temporal scaffolds in this pilot setting, while leaving open the possibility of subtler semantic anchoring effects. We contribute an audit framework and anonymized interaction traces for studying when AI-assisted annotation preserves, reshapes, or collapses human disagreement.

papers.title: HapBO: Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization via Expert Natural Language Priors
papers.summary: Bayesian Optimization (BO) can be substantially more sample-efficient when informed by prior knowledge about the problem. In practice, however, such knowledge is often available only in natural language, e.g., expert intuitions or documentation, rather than as the explicit probability distribution landscape that prior-guided BO methods may require. Leveraging it effectively demands both an expressive mapping from language to priors and robustness to information that may be misleading. We propose HapBO (Harnessed $α$-$π$ Bayesian Optimization), which elicits beliefs once from a human expert, a large language model (LLM), or both, and deterministically compiles a structured specification into a reusable belief function ($π: \mathcal{X} \to[0,1]$), with a rich representation not restricted to a Gaussian family. Building on $α$-$π$BO, HapBO applies this belief function through a bounded positive multiplier on any nonnegative acquisition, preserving positive acquisition support and requiring no LLM calls during optimization. We prove that, for the Expected Improvement acquisition function (EI), HapBO preserves the standard simple-regret rate up to a bounded factor, even under adversarial beliefs. We evaluate HapBO on 40 HPOBench tasks, a synthetic suite in 6-15 dimensions and two real-world applications: cortical neurostimulation and constrained solar design. HapBO achieves the lowest aggregate HPOBench regret and strong real-world task performance, with zero in-loop token cost. In real-world applications it improves the optimization outcome even at budgets of 12-20 queries, and at a small fraction of the wall-clock and token costs of other LLM-based methods.

papers.title: Component-Adaptive and Lesion-Level Supervision for Improved Small Structure Segmentation in Brain MRI
papers.summary: Small lesions in brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are easily missed: a segmentation model can reach a high Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) while leaving many of them undetected. We ask whether this omission comes from the network or from the training objective. In multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation, nnU-Net trained with its default Dice and cross-entropy loss produces almost no response to most of the small lesions it misses, so no decision threshold recovers them, and four other architectures trained with the same loss detect no more of them. We therefore change only the objective. CATMIL adds two lesion-level terms to the nnU-Net loss: a Component-Adaptive Tversky (CAT) term, which gives each lesion a weight nearly independent of its size, and a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) term, which treats each lesion as a bag of voxels and penalizes any lesion in which no voxel is detected. On MSLesSeg, CATMIL raises small-lesion recall from 0.796 to 0.873 (difference 95\% CI +0.030 to +0.157) and misses 48\% fewer lesions, at comparable DSC. The gain holds on the cross-validation predictions of 47 further patients, for lesions of at least 3~mm, and on a second dataset trained with the same loss weights. CATMIL also detects more small lesions than CC-DiceCE, an instance-level loss that balances lesions within an overlap term (0.873 vs.\ 0.831), indicating that lesions must be supervised not only in proportion but also for their detection. The cost is additional small false-positive components; a component-size filter removes most of them, and at the lesion-wise precision of the default loss CATMIL still detects more small lesions. papers.title: PriTabICL: Differentially Private Tabular In-Context Learning with Task-Aligned Cluster-Wise Synthesis
papers.summary: Tabular in-context learning (TabICL) enables large language models (LLMs) to predict target records using a handful of labeled demonstrations in their prompts. However, these demonstrations often contain sensitive personal information. Differential privacy (DP) offers principled protection, but noise-based methods introduce substantial noise, distorting the feature-label relationships essential for accurate prediction, especially as data dimensionality grows. In this work, we study DP data synthesis for generating privacy-preserving TabICL demonstrations. We identify two limitations of directly applying general-purpose DP synthesis to entire datasets: modeling a global distribution can obscure local structure and minority patterns in heterogeneous data, while measuring broad attribute dependencies under a limited privacy budget can reduce the accuracy available for relationships most relevant to prediction. More broadly, global statistical fidelity may fail to preserve heterogeneous structures needed by downstream predictive and generative models. To address these challenges, we propose PriTabICL, a general framework compatible with existing DP synthesis algorithms. It partitions records into DP clusters and synthesizes each independently, using a fixed feature-target workload to prioritize prediction-relevant statistical relationships. At inference, each query is routed to a DP cluster, and demonstrations are sampled from its synthetic dataset without additional privacy loss for the original records. Experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our methods across heterogeneous datasets. In particular, one of our instantiations, PriTabICL-PrivSyn, improves over global PrivSyn in 8 out of 12 settings and outperforms existing private TabICL approaches in nearly all evaluated settings. Open-source code is available.

papers.title: Observable Performance Does Not Fully Reflect Adaptive System Organization: A Multi-Level Analysis of Gait Dynamics Under Occlusal Constraint
papers.summary: In biomechanical systems, observable performance is often used as a proxy for underlying organization, although similar outputs may arise from different adaptive configurations. OC2.5 and OC3 displayed limited centroid displacement but broad observation-level overlap. papers.title: Is Randomness Necessary for Adaptive Data Analysis?
papers.summary: The Adaptive Data Analysis (ADA) problem formalizes the challenge of preventing false discovery and overfitting when a dataset is repeatedly reused. Formally, our input is a dataset containing $n$ i.i.d. samples from an unknown distribution $\mathcal{P}$ over a domain $\mathcal{X}$, and our goal is to answer a sequence of $k$ adaptively chosen statistical queries with respect to $\mathcal{P}$. The main question is how many queries we can support (i.e., how large $k$ can be), primarily as a function of the number of samples $n$. This question has been intensively studied and is relatively well-understood for randomized mechanisms: there are computationally efficient mechanisms that support $k \approx n^2$ queries, and no computationally efficient mechanism can answer $k \gg n^2$ queries. In this paper, we address a fundamental question: is randomness necessary for ADA? Despite a decade of work on ADA, this question remains open. A folklore observation dating back to the initial works on ADA is that randomness is {\em not} necessary when the analyst is computationally bounded. Yet, the necessity of randomness against computationally unbounded analysts has remained elusive. Our main contribution resolves this gap in the information-theoretic setting. Perhaps surprisingly, we show that randomness is {\em strictly necessary} to answer a non-trivial number of adaptive queries: when the analyst is unbounded, any deterministic mechanism can be forced to fail after just $k = \tilde{O}(n)$ queries.

papers.title: Bigger Isn't Always Memorizing: Early Stopping Overparameterized Diffusion Models
papers.summary: Diffusion probabilistic models have become a cornerstone of modern generative AI, yet the mechanisms underlying their generalization remain poorly understood. In fact, if these models were perfectly minimizing their training loss, they would just generate data belonging to their training set, i.e., memorize, as empirically found in the overparameterized regime. We revisit this view by showing that, in highly overparameterized diffusion models, generalization in natural data domains is progressively achieved during training before the onset of memorization. Our results, ranging from image to language diffusion models, systematically support the empirical law that memorization time is proportional to the dataset size, consistent with a kernel-regression bound on the time required to fit the empirical score at low noise. Generalization vs. memorization is then best understood as a competition between time scales. We show that this phenomenology is recovered in diffusion models learning a simple probabilistic context-free grammar with random rules, where generalization corresponds to the hierarchical acquisition of deeper grammar rules as training time grows, and the generalization cost of early stopping can be characterized. We summarize these results in a phase diagram. Overall, our results support that a principled early-stopping criterion - scaling with dataset size - can effectively optimize generalization while avoiding memorization, with direct implications for hyperparameter transfer and privacy-sensitive applications.

papers.title: Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation
papers.summary: We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization. We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement, and analyze their joint SGD dynamics together with the second layer in the proportional limit. We show that although SGD updates to the complement are initially isotropic, the training dynamics induce teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix. This emergent anisotropy provides a concrete mechanism by which representation variance is amplified, and generalization degrades. To isolate this effect, we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD. In simulations with a ReLU student, freezing the directions of the orthogonal complement improves generalization relative to training them. Finally, we show that the signal component rapidly aligns with the second-layer weights, revealing strong cross-layer coupling even in this shallow setting. Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.

papers.title: Monoculture Robust Learning
papers.summary: We introduce a notion of monoculture robustness in Probably Approximately Correct (PAC) learning, as a way to mitigate the problem of algorithmic monoculture (Kleinberg and Raghavan, 2021): the tendency of models sharing the same components (e.g., training data) to fail on the same inputs. Specifically, we ask whether a learner with access to a single dataset can output $k$ individually accurate hypotheses whose joint failure probability is comparable to training on $k$ independent datasets. We say that such a learning procedure achieves monoculture robustness, and we quantify this by bounding the conjunctive error that all $k$ hypotheses misclassify points in an individual sense. We design methods for achieving this type of guarantee by drawing a surprising connection between replicability (Impagliazzo et al., 2022) and monoculture robustness. Specifically, we show that if the base learner is $ρ$-replicable, then running it independently $k$ times on the same sample yields individual monoculture error that shrinks exponentially with $k$, controlled by the single-run error of the base learner at the point and $ρ$. We complement these positive results with a lower bound: for individual monoculture robustness, we prove a worst-case lower bound showing that, for learners, driving the individual conjunctive error down to $γ$ can require a sample-size multiplier of $t = Ω(\log(1/γ))$.

papers.title: TangentPDE: Learning Local Operator Responses with Sparse Finite-Difference Supervision
papers.summary: Neural PDE operators are often optimized through state reconstruction, which largely constrains operator values at observed inputs but does not fully characterize their sensitivity to local perturbations. Its objective jointly constrains state fidelity, response-direction alignment, and response-magnitude calibration, thereby learning both operator values and their local variations. Because the response labels are constructed solely from state outputs at paired inputs, the method requires neither explicit derivative labels, linearized or adjoint PDE solves, nor full Jacobians, and remains applicable to nonlinear solvers without derivative interfaces. Budget-matched and correspondence-perturbed controls isolate the effect of relational supervision from improvements attributable to additional state observations or increased data volume. papers.title: Overlooked and Underutilized: Prototypes are the Missing Piece in Tabular XAI
papers.summary: Explainable AI (XAI) is frequently applied to high-stakes tabular data, yet the field relies heavily on feature attribution methods. While these approaches offer technical transparency, evaluating dozens of isolated features demands excessive cognitive effort from non-expert users. Although entire exemplars function as an intuitive baseline for prototype-based explanations, we highlight prototypical parts as particularly valuable for tabular data. By grouping related features into bounded subspaces, prototypical parts technically embody human-understandable concepts, replacing isolated features with cohesive semantic units. We support this integration through two primary lenses. Cognitively, these parts align with Rosch's categorization theory and Kahneman's System 1 thinking to naturally reduce cognitive load for humans. Then, we introduce a Geometric Validity Triad to conceptualize why prototypes validate the data manifold - a critical dimension often neglected by existing methods. We contend that making tabular XAI genuinely comprehensible requires shifting toward composite explanation pipelines that pair intuitive similarity-based reasoning with rigorous feature-level auditing. The paper concludes by outlining open challenges of prototype-based methods and discussing potential solutions to guide future research.

papers.title: TROPT: An Open Framework for Unifying and Advancing Discrete Text Optimization
papers.summary: Discrete text-trigger optimization -- searching for text sequences that, when ingested by a model, steer it toward a specified objective -- underpins model red-teaming (e.g., LLM jailbreaks), as well as auditing and interpretability. TROPT currently ships with 40+ optimization recipes -- covering applications such as jailbreaking and probing model internals -- built from 15+ optimizers (spanning white-box to black-box access) and 15+ losses, from foundational to state-of-the-art methods. papers.title: Minimum Neural Weight Norm = Kolmogorov Complexity
papers.summary: Why do neural networks generalize better when their parameter norm is small? We prove that, in looped neural networks with constant-precision weights, the smallest weight norm of a network computing a function is asymptotically equivalent to the Kolmogorov complexity of that function, divided by its logarithm. The proof has two reductions: looped neural networks can encode information at a rate of logarithmically many bits per non-zero parameter encoded via the sparsity pattern, while any fixed-precision network can be described by enumerating its non-zero parameters with logarithmic addressing cost. Both bounds have the same leading constant factors, giving an asymptotic equivalence. More broadly, by establishing a theoretical link between norm minimization and algorithmic simplicity, we provide an avenue towards understanding generalization in modern deep learning.

papers.title: Sparse designs via quantization of the uniform measure on high-dimensional hypercubes
papers.summary: While the notions of sphere packing and sphere covering underlie the most widely used criteria for space-filling design in computer experiments, namely, the maximin and minimax approaches, they suffer from major drawbacks in high dimensions. First, when the dimension $d$ is very large, deploying a space-filling design requires an extremely large number of design points, making the very notion of a space-filling design questionable. Second, these two design characteristics are highly sensitive to boundaries, particularly when the design domain is a hypercube (the case considered in this paper), and especially to its vertices. This sensitivity is particularly acute when the design size is less than $2^d$. Instead of considering the maximin or minimax criterion, we consider here the quantization error of the uniform measure on the hypercube. This error has three key advantages: it accounts for the entire distribution of distances from a random point $U$ to the design, is less sensitive to boundary effects than the maximin and minimax criteria, and, thanks to Zador's celebrated theorem, enables a smooth and natural transition to uniform designs as the design size tends to infinity. Building on recent results on the construction of optimal random quantizers for spherically symmetric distributions (arXiv:2610.11772) we propose a method to generate random designs of a given target size $n$ with small $L_s$-mean quantization error. The support of the resulting distribution is then used to construct designs, possibly incrementally, with sizes up to $n$. We demonstrate that, for moderate $n$, designs supported on a fractional factorial subset of the vertices of a small hypercube perform exceptionally well---and significantly better than designs uniformly distributed over the entire hypercube. We also explain how to account for projections onto lower-dimensional subspaces.

papers.title: Targeted Synthetic Control Method
papers.summary: The synthetic control method (SCM) estimates causal effects in panel data with a single-treated unit by constructing a counterfactual outcome as a weighted combination of untreated control units that matches the pre-treatment trajectory. papers.title: Every Query Routes Itself: Accelerating Video Diffusion Transformers with Per-Query Routed Sparse Attention
papers.summary: Self-attention over long token sequences dominates the inference cost of video diffusion transformers. papers.title: PoCoFL: A Framework for POlicy-COmpliant Federated Learning
papers.summary: Federated Learning (FL) is a privacy-oriented learning paradigm that enables collaborative model training while keeping training data local to clients. However, FL does not guarantee that clients submit policy-compliant contributions or that aggregators process admitted contributions correctly. Update-magnitude bounds alone cannot ensure compliance with learning-specific requirements involving private data, intermediate models, or retained state. These requirements differ across FL settings, motivating a unified framework to specify and verify client and aggregation policies. This work introduces PoCoFL, a policy-compliant federated learning framework that separates three aspects: (i) FL type, (ii) policy semantics, and (iii) cryptographic realisation. We provide a formalisation that captures client and aggregation requirements as policy-dependent relations, defining update admissibility, aggregation correctness, and policy-relative privacy. These relations enable verification of selected properties of intermediate objects, such as local-model loss, continual-learning state, and personalised optimisation conditions, in each round. Clients demonstrate compliance of their contributions using compatible cryptographic mechanisms, while aggregators prove that the recorded set of admitted contributions was processed according to the selected aggregation policy. We demonstrate PoCoFL through four formal instantiations and corresponding proof-of-concept realisations: (i) vanilla, (ii) continual, (iii) personalised, and (iv) threshold-encrypted federated learning. We evaluate how policy enforcement affects the learning objectives of vanilla, personalised, and continual FL, and quantify the computational and communication overhead of policy verification across all four instantiations. These results demonstrate that PoCoFL captures complex policy representations across the evaluated FL settings.

papers.title: Statistical Taylor Expansion: A New and Path-Independent Method for Uncertainty Analysis
papers.summary: Statistical Taylor expansion is a rigorous extension of conventional Taylor expansion that replaces each precise input variable with a random variable of known distribution and sample count, then computes the mean, deviation, and a bounding reliability of every result. This study also reveals the potentially substantial impact of numerical errors in library functions, the defect of applying input uncertainties as weights in conventional regression, and the modeling error of the discrete Fourier transformation. papers.title: Are You Learning Biological Signal or Shortcuts? Auditing and Mitigating Bias in Protein-Protein Interaction Datasets
papers.summary: Protein-protein interaction (PPI) databases do not faithfully reflect biological realities. Instead, they are influenced by study and technical biases that distort certain protein and interaction attributes. To detect and mitigate these biases, we provide an open Nextflow pipeline that combines similarity-aware, data-loss-minimizing dataset splitting with bias-minimizing negative sampling, both formulated as integer linear programs. papers.title: ReCALM: A Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism for Distributed Continual Service Construction
papers.summary: Crowdsourcing has emerged as a promising paradigm for constructing AI services by harnessing the collective capabilities of distributed workers. As consumers' demands continually evolve, service models must acquire new knowledge while retaining previously learned information. However, due to the inherited reliance on gradients for backpropagation, existing approaches typically suffer from catastrophic forgetting during continual model updates on heterogeneous data. Recent studies have introduced analytic learning, a gradient-free paradigm that achieves invariance through recursive closed-form solutions. Nevertheless, existing analytic methods are typically constrained by single-layer linear networks, which tend to suffer from underfitting due to their inability to perform deep representation learning. To address this issue, we propose ReCALM, a Residual-enhanced Crowdsourced Analytic Learning Mechanism that achieves deep nonlinear invariance for distributed continual service construction. Inspired by the success of ResNet, we develop gradient-free residual blocks for ReCALM with closed-form solutions. To implement distributed continual training for ReCALM, we further devise a cross-recursive strategy via least squares. Both theoretical and experimental analyses verify ReCALM's dual superiority in heterogeneity invariance and deep representation. With 20 residual layers, ReCALM improves accuracy by 8.85%-9.83% over the single-layer analytic baseline, while reducing computational costs by over 94% compared with gradient-based baselines.

papers.title: LoopCache: Accelerating Long-Context Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Transformers
papers.summary: Looped Transformers achieve large effective depth with compact models by repeatedly applying a weight-shared block across R recurrent steps, each maintaining a loop-specific key-value (KV) cache. To accelerate sequential loop execution, recent wave-style self-speculative methods like WaveFront Decoding (WFD) and LoopSpec pipeline draft and target tokens across loops in a single step. However, they face two critical limitations. First, they draft only at fixed loops and ignore intermediate prediction changes, wasting computation on stale trajectories. Second, batching tokens from different loops loads up to Rx the KV cache per step, severely amplifying memory traffic in long-context scenarios. To address these challenges, we propose LoopCache, an efficient self-speculative decoding framework for long-context Looped Transformers. Based on the correlation between prediction switches and output confidence, LoopCache introduces confidence-guided dynamic draft updating to refine drafts in flight across all intermediate loops. Furthermore, LoopCache employs a cyclic loop KV cache strategy that rotates through loop-specific KV caches, restricting per-step KV traffic to a single loop while batching tokens at the nearest matching cycle for lossless verification. By also selectively retaining independent KV caches for a few loop-sensitive shallow layers, LoopCache improves acceptance rates with negligible overhead. Experiments show that LoopCache achieves average 10.25x and 14.56x speedup over WFD and LoopSpec.

papers.title: Stability-compatible kernels: beyond Gaussianity for impulse response estimation
papers.summary: Kernel-based regularization for linear system identification uses positive semidefinite kernels both to define reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHSs) and as covariance models for stochastic impulse responses. Sharp kernel conditions are known for RKHS stability, while almost-sure BIBO stability under Gaussian priors requires an even more restrictive covariance condition. These restrictions, however, need not persist beyond Gaussianity, where the covariance no longer determines the full probability law. We introduce the notion of a stability-compatible kernel, namely a covariance kernel admitting at least one stochastic realization with almost-surely absolutely summable sample paths. We show that stability-compatibility holds if and only if the stable elements are dense in the associated RKHS, a condition strictly weaker than RKHS stability, and derive practical sufficient conditions, including a spectral criterion for stationary kernels. We then construct non-Gaussian priors that preserve a prescribed covariance while enforcing almost-sure stability. In particular, this yields a stable prior based on the stationary radial-basis-function (RBF) kernel, separating covariance structure from the mechanism enforcing stability. Numerical experiments show substantial estimation gains for several important classes of impulse responses, with particularly pronounced advantages when relevant dynamics occur at late lags or in separated temporal regions.

papers.title: MUSE: Multi-Tenant Model Serving With Seamless Model Updates
papers.summary: In binary classification systems, decision thresholds translate model scores into actions. Choosing suitable thresholds relies on the specific distribution of the underlying model scores but also on the specific business decisions of each client using that model. However, retraining models inevitably shifts score distributions, invalidating existing thresholds. In multi-tenant Score-as-a-Service environments, where decision boundaries reside in client-managed infrastructure, this creates a severe bottleneck: recalibration requires coordinating threshold updates across hundreds of clients, consuming excessive human hours and leading to model stagnation. We introduce MUSE, a model serving framework that enables seamless model updates by decoupling model scores from client decision boundaries. Designed for multi-tenancy, MUSE optimizes infrastructure re-use by sharing models via dynamic intent-based routing, combined with a two-level score transformation that maps model outputs to a stable, reference distribution. Deployed at scale by Feedzai, MUSE processes over 4 thousand events per second, and over 55 billion events in the last 12 months, across several dozens of tenants, while maintaining high-availability and low-latency guarantees. By reducing model lead time from weeks to minutes, MUSE promotes model resilience against shifting attacks, saving millions of dollars in fraud losses and operational costs.

papers.title: Explanations that Transfer: Interpreting Medical Retrieval with Sparse AutoEncoders
papers.summary: Medical AI systems that answer users' queries rely on retrieving medical knowledge from large document collections. In this context, finetuning general models on medical datasets can improve retrieval relevance. Yet the dense embeddings underlying modern retrieval systems remain largely opaque, making it difficult to understand the mechanics behind their results. Moreover, adapting to a specific medical dataset risks losing transferability to new clinical corpora. In this work, we tackle these issues by applying Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to medical information retrieval, transforming dense text embeddings into semantically interpretable representations. To do so, our model combines a reconstruction objective with an InfoNCE contrastive loss that directly preserves query-document relevance. We evaluate three embedding models across six medical retrieval datasets, both in-domain and out-of-domain. Trained on a medical corpus, our sparse codes improve in-domain retrieval over the original embeddings, and lose less out-of-domain performance than their dense counterparts, especially when the target corpus is distant from the training one. Importantly, our experiments show that the method yields interpretable features whose semantic content can be inferred from the queries and documents that activate them most strongly. The interpretation of these features sheds light on why a particular document was retrieved, and transfers beyond the training distribution.

papers.title: Training-Free Dynamic Upcycling of Expert Language Models
papers.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance on a wide range of specialized tasks, exhibiting strong problem-solving capabilities. However, training these models is prohibitively expensive, and they often lack domain-specific expertise because they rely on general knowledge datasets. Expertise finetuning can address this issue; however, it often leads to overspecialization, and developing a single multi-domain expert remains difficult due to diverging objectives. Furthermore, multitask training is challenging due to interference and catastrophic forgetting. Existing work proposes combining the expertise of dense models within a Mixture of Experts (MoE) architecture, although this approach still requires multitask finetuning. To address these issues, we introduce Dynamic Upcycling MoE (DUME), a novel approach that reuses dense experts trained on different domains to construct a unified MoE model. Our method builds a single multitask model that preserves the capabilities of the original dense experts without requiring additional training. DUME is both cost-efficient and scalable: by leveraging the closed-form solution of ridge regression, it eliminates the need for further optimization and enables experts to be added or removed dynamically. Our extensive experiments on different tasks (in causal language modeling and reasoning settings) with several model sizes (between 115M and 9B parameters) and architectures demonstrate that DUME consistently outperforms baseline approaches. In particular, in a reasoning setting, DUME can also surpass the dense expert model's performance in its domain, achieving 104% of the dense expert's performance on average. Finally, we also show that the DUME model can be fine-tuned to further improve performance in complex reasoning scenarios. Our code is available at: github.com/gensyn-ai/dume.

papers.title: TRESS: A Fixed-Size History Representation for Irregular Time Series Forecasting
papers.summary: A fixed number of recent observations may span minutes for one variable and days for another. Earlier measurements can still reveal whether the latest value is unusual for that variable. We propose TRESS (Timestamped Recent Events and Statistical Summaries), a forecasting model that retains the latest observations at their original times and summarises the full history of each variable. For a given set of variables and event budget, this representation stays the same size as the record grows. Its query-conditioned event lifting module weights deviations from the latest value according to the age of each observation and the forecast horizon. A channel-specific decoder combines the resulting features with historical statistics and a summary shared across variables to predict a correction to the latest value. Retaining 8 to 16 observations per variable, TRESS records the lowest mean test MSE and MAE among the methods compared on all four benchmarks. Serving 32 successive query times from one encoded history reduces CPU inference time by a factor of 2.12--2.60 across the four datasets. The code is at https://github.com/SSMa913/NICLab-TRESS.

papers.title: ViLFlow: Parallel Vision-Language Generation with Continuous Latent Flows
papers.summary: Vision-language generation has predominantly relied on autoregressive and discrete diffusion models. Autoregressive models generate tokens sequentially, while discrete diffusion models typically predict tokens independently within each denoising step. We propose ViLFlow (Vision-Language Flow), a continuous-flow vision-language model that combines joint modeling of output embeddings with parallel token decoding. ViLFlow adapts pretrained continuous language generation to visual question answering and image captioning through learned image guidance and prediction-aware token decoding. A visually adapted teacher provides image-guided predictions as additional denoising supervision. The denoiser learns to reproduce these predictions directly, retaining one image-conditioned prediction per generation step. We train the token decoder on denoiser predictions and paired reference text to improve the conversion of continuous outputs into words. The decoder can be adapted independently, improving answering and captioning without further denoiser training. For captioning, it also supplies text feedback during late denoising, allowing decoded words to inform subsequent refinement. ViLFlow outperforms autoregressive and masked-diffusion baselines by up to 8.46 percentage points on VQAv2 and 4.50 points on GQA without GQA training. On COCO Karpathy test, it improves CIDEr by 16.25 over masked diffusion and 17.81 over sampled autoregression.

papers.title: Functional Principal Component Analysis: Minimax Optimality from Sparse to Dense Designs and Beyond
papers.summary: Functional principal component analysis (FPCA) plays a central role as a dimension-reduction and representation tool in functional data analysis, but its minimax theory for diverging spectral indices under noisy discrete observation has remained open for over two decades. To fill this gap, we consider a sieve-based FPCA framework that pools discrete measurements across subjects and accommodates sampling frequencies ranging from sparse to dense under random designs. We begin by establishing new minimax rates for covariance estimation over general bivariate function classes beyond tensor-product low-complexity structures, thereby identifying the intrinsically two-dimensional optimal rate. Our central theoretical contribution is to establish minimax optimal rates for both individually labelled eigenfunctions with diverging indices and leading principal subspaces of increasing dimensions, under explicit growth and regularity conditions. To establish these results, we develop a general framework for sharp minimax analysis of FPCA under discrete observation, separating spectral approximation from stochastic perturbations and exploiting their distinct structures, thereby offering a new approach to a broad class of nonparametric spectral estimation problems. For both spectral targets, the optimal rates reveal two distinct statistical mechanisms, spectral identification and nonparametric reconstruction, whose interplay gives rise to either four or two sampling regimes. This yields, for the first time, a precise characterization of the impact of discrete sampling across the full range from sparse to dense designs. Finally, as a downstream application, we analyze FPCA-based functional linear regression and show that the FPCA-based estimator attains the minimax-optimal rates.

papers.title: Continuous Noisy-Loop Models
papers.summary: Efficient learning and inference need not imply a compact probabilistic circuit. We quantify this distinction for continuous noisy readings of agreement between adjacent latent spins on a known square grid with $d$ edges. With known margins and bounded Lipschitz channels, minimax squared Hellinger risk is $Θ(\min\{1,dN^{-2/3}\})$ from $N$ independent vectors, without a reliability lower bound. A spline estimator reaches this rate in polynomial arithmetic time given a fixed positive reliability bound; an exponential-size mixture removes that requirement. At fixed positive reliability, nonnegative decomposable circuits need $\exp(Θ(\sqrt d))$ nodes for fixed total-variation error below one, even when each leaf uses at most $αd$ coordinates, $0<α<1$. Optimal Kullback--Leibler (KL) approximation error is $Θ(d/\max\{\log d,\sqrt\ell\})$ in either direction with at most $d^r$ nodes and leaf scopes $\ell\leqαd$, for fixed $r>1$ and $0<α<2/3$. Node counts exclude leaf computation. For three fixed masks, optimal joint conditional KL has order $d/\log d$ when $\ell\leq(\log d)^2$. Local cycle identities relate joint divergence to identifiable channel products and separate weak-channel recovery from density estimation. Factorized evidence preserves a planar zero-field Ising model: given local integrals, exact queries cost $O(d^{3/2})$ arithmetic operations and one root extraction.

papers.title: When Is Accuracy Evidence? A Unified Theory of Generalisation, Validation, and Information Fusion
papers.summary: K-fold cross-validation (CV) is widely used as evidence of out-of-sample performance, although folds are neither independent experiments nor equally informative under heterogeneous data. Cross Upper-Bound Validation (CUBV) replaces point-wise CV accuracy by conservative upper bounds on true risk. Here we generalise CUBV through a single exponential framework in which the moment-generating function of the generalisation gap is controlled by a cumulant envelope gamma(lambda). This yields a family of risk bounds covering Hoeffding-, Bernstein-, dependency-aware, PAC-Bayesian, and heterogeneous source-fusion settings. For K-fold CV, dependence between fold-wise gaps is modelled through a joint sub-Gaussian proxy matrix. Under equicorrelation, this gives an effective number of folds, Keff = K/[1+(K-1)rho], showing that increasing K does not necessarily increase statistical evidence when folds are strongly dependent. The framework is also extended to posterior distributions over predictors and weighted multi-source fusion, where weights are selected by minimising an upper bound on future risk rather than empirical error alone. Experiments with trained linear classifiers on heterogeneous multimodal Gaussian mixtures compare K-fold CV with full-sample resubstitution plus risk correction. Bounds are evaluated by coverage and tightness. In low-dimensional small-sample settings, K-fold partitioning can increase uncertainty because individual folds under-represent minority modes, while corrected resubstitution can remain valid and tighter; this effect disappears as sample size increases. Overall, gamma-CUBV separates observed performance, uncertainty, dependence, model complexity, and confidence into explicit terms, providing a unified route from CV scores to risk statements and a principled validation criterion for heterogeneous small-sample applications such as neuroimaging.

papers.title: Optimistic Actor-Critic with Parametric Policies for Linear Markov Decision Processes
papers.summary: Although actor-critic methods have been successful in practice, their theoretical analyses have several limitations. Specifically, existing theoretical work either sidesteps the exploration problem by making strong assumptions or analyzes impractical methods with complicated algorithmic modifications. Moreover, the actor-critic methods analyzed for linear MDPs often employ natural policy gradient and define "implicit" policies through the accumulated critic estimates, rather than learning an explicitly parameterized actor. Such policies can be computationally expensive to sample from, making the environment interactions inefficient. To that end, we focus on the finite-horizon linear MDPs and propose an optimistic actor-critic framework that uses parametric log-linear policies. In particular, we introduce a tractable logit-matching regression objective for the actor. For the critic, we use approximate Thompson sampling via Langevin Monte Carlo to obtain optimistic value estimates. We prove that, when the policy features are sufficiently expressive, the resulting algorithm achieves $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-4})$ and $\widetilde{O}(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity in the on-policy and off-policy settings, respectively. Our results match the state-of-the-art dependence on $ε$ in prior theoretical work, while our algorithm is more aligned with practice.

papers.title: Learning with Unlearning: Synaptic Role Partitioning for Simultaneous Continual Learning and Machine Unlearning
papers.summary: Continual Learning (CL) asks a model to acquire new knowledge without forgetting what it already knows. Machine Unlearning (MU) asks it to destroy specific knowledge without damaging the rest. The challenge is integrating them in the same system; the two objectives pull on the same weights, and an edit made for one harms the other. To address this, we propose Learning with Unlearning (LwU), a unified framework that resolves the conflict where it occurs: at the individual synapse. LwU scores every weight twice, once against the data to keep and once against the data to delete, and partitions the network into four zones with separate update rules. Weights that only require retention are frozen. Weights that only require deletion are cleared and returned to the network as free capacity. Contested weights take a gradient-ascent step projected orthogonally to the retention gradient. The remaining capacity learns the incoming task by a privileged teacher via self-distillation. Deletion is served post hoc, and no retraining is required. Across both CL and MU jobs, LwU outperforms or matches the strongest baseline. Its real-world practicality has been demonstrated on the Physical Artificial Intelligence (PAI) dataset we conducted. Additionally, in the image generation task and in removing dangerous content, it outperformed the closest baseline, as shown in Fig.1.

papers.title: Rare-Tail Statistics For Learning Biased Gaussian Halfspaces with Label Noise
papers.summary: We revisit the classical problem of learning general Gaussian halfspaces in the presence of label noise, with particular focus on the large-bias regime, where information-computation gaps are conjectured in several standard label-noise models. Concretely, we present and analyze the rare-tail mean estimator, an extremely simple one-shot statistic that averages only the observed minority class. In the large-bias regime, classical Averaging (Servedio, 1999) and related global first-moment statistics are provably suboptimal, while the rare-tail mean estimator recovers the target halfspace direction at the information-theoretic sample rate (modulo log factors) under a broad class of label noise models, including probit noise and margin-dependent noise with very slow decay away from the boundary. Notably, our guarantees allow labels arbitrarily close to the decision boundary to be nearly random, while still giving strong directional recovery from a small number of samples. The estimator also cleanly interpolates between the noiseless and noisy regimes: without noise, it attains the same sample rate as classical separability-based methods for realizable halfspaces, and under low noise, or noise that decays away from the boundary, it keeps this rate even after linear separability has been destroyed. As an application, we consider a two-stage curriculum in which source samples, whose noise may be arbitrarily close to $1/2$ near the boundary and decay very slowly away from it, precede target samples, whose noise flips every label at the same rate, i.e., random classification noise (RCN). Since both stages share the same Bayes optimal halfspace, our estimator supplies the directional warm start needed by existing refinement routines, and together they learn the RCN target at the information-theoretic sample rate in the large-bias regime, up to log factors.

papers.title: SoU-RHS: Bayesian Structured Sparsity for Compact Architecture Recovery in CNNs

papers.title: Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Causal Function Recovery under Network Interference
papers.summary: Causal inference seeks to learn how outcomes change under alternative interventions, but network interactions complicate this task. Under network interference, outcomes depend on both own treatment and neighbors' treatments, making causal effects functions of neighborhood exposure rather than single treatment contrasts. Existing methods primarily target prespecified causal contrasts or their estimation precision, leaving global response-function recovery largely unexplored. We study sequential experimentation under a limited experimental budget, with the goal of recovering the full exposure-dependent population-average response function. To this end, we propose FANCI (Fill-Distance-Guided Active Learning for Network-Interference Causal Inference). For function learning, treatment-specific Gaussian processes flexibly model nonlinear conditional response surfaces. For experimental design, we formulate global response-function recovery as a coverage problem and propose a fill-distance criterion that guides new experiments toward poorly covered regions. To account for network constraints on attainable exposure patterns, we develop full-network and target-screened strategies for selecting feasible network--assignment pairs. Theoretically, we derive uniform error bounds linking fill distance to response-function estimation and characterize the approximation loss from target screening. Simulations and an online-game experiment show that FANCI improves recovery of nonlinear exposure-dependent effects and reveals treatment patterns obscured when network interference is ignored.

papers.title: QuantAtlas-OM: Taming Neural Spectral Bias in Long-Horizon Spatiotemporal Ocean Dynamics
papers.summary: Autoregressive neural networks exhibit spectral bias in long-horizon spatiotemporal prediction. As rollouts progress, high-frequency details decay, blurring the predicted fields and destabilizing long-range forecasts. Ocean dynamics offer a particularly stringent test because kinetic energy is concentrated in mesoscale eddies and fronts spanning tens of kilometers. This degradation stems from coupling large-scale phase evolution and small-scale energy retention in a shared feature space. Evolution on a coarse grid smooths out high-wavenumber eddies, whereas evolution on a fine grid amplifies small-scale phase errors and triggers rollout instability. We introduce QuantAtlas-OM (QuantAtlas Ocean Model), a scale-spectral decoupling framework that confines deep temporal evolution to a low-wavenumber latent manifold for long-term stability while routing full-resolution eddy and front residuals through an outer bypass to the decoder. Across physical regimes, the evolution core pairs non-local attention with resolution-invariant dilated spatial gating. Across three western boundary currents, QuantAtlas-OM retains $43.7\%$ to $86.5\%$ of mesoscale spectral energy along the $k^{-3}$ cascade at Day $120$, sustains anomaly correlation coefficients of $0.81$ to $0.88$ at Day $60$, and reaches $0.66$ at Day $120$ in the Kuroshio ($2.5\times$ to $7.7\times$ the best baselines). papers.title: Uncertainty-aware damage identification in short-span bridges via physics-informed variational autoencoder
papers.summary: Vibration-based damage identification in civil infrastructure is a challenging, ill-posed inverse problem due to measurement noise, sparse sensor arrays, and modeling errors. The methodology introduces two main contributions. First, a numerical eigenvalue solver is embedded directly into the variational autoencoder as its decoder, which replaces data-driven surrogates, ensures that every posterior sample satisfies the governing equations of structural dynamics, and reduces the number of trainable parameters. Second, a Gaussian copula describes the posterior distribution of the stiffness factors, capturing cross-correlations between components with fewer parameters than Gaussian mixtures in real time. The method estimates the posterior distribution of the damage condition, i.e., the stiffness reduction factors of the deck zones and bearings, and these posteriors closely match the exact ones computed with sequential Monte Carlo sampling. The results reveal that the proposed methodology offers a robust and interpretable decision-making tool, able not only to indicate the presence and location of damage, but also to inform on the uncertainty associated with the diagnosis, for instance, when light damage is masked by the effect of noise or when the measured modal properties present limited sensitivity to damage.

papers.title: Pareto-Informed Smart "Predict, then Optimize" for Multi-Objective Combinatorial Problems
papers.summary: Many real-world planning applications, from logistics, routing to resource allocation, give rise to optimization problems that need to balance multiple, conflicting objectives. While machine learning is often used to predict the unknown parameters or costs of these problems, standard models trained on prediction accuracy can lead to suboptimal plans. Decision-Focused Learning (DFL) addresses this by integrating the downstream optimization task into the training objective. However, existing DFL methods for multi-objective problems rely on simple scalarization, which fails to capture the rich trade-offs of the Pareto Frontier. To address this gap, we propose a Pareto-aware extension to single-objective Smart "Predict, then Optimize" (SPO+) for multi-objective combinatorial optimization problems. papers.title: Algorithmic Market Making Can Lead to Rough Volatility Through the Order Book

We confirm the key predictions of the model on simulated agents and on six months of Binance data with about 790 million orders. papers.title: One Checkpoint, Many Runs: Recipe Cards for Fine-Tuned Models
papers.summary: Fine-tuned language models are shared with model cards that describe the training setup in detail, often down to the default random seed, but report the score of a single released checkpoint. Such setups are retrained routinely, by fine-tuning services for each customer, by organizations at each update, and by users on their own data, so the model that is deployed comes from a new run of the setup. Some runs fail, and a failed run can go unnoticed and reach the people the model serves. We call such a setup a model recipe and argue that its documentation should state how often a run of the recipe misses a required performance bar. Across 2,124 fine-tuning runs, we find that reading the mean, the median, or a bootstrap interval as an approval often approves recipes whose failure rate exceeds a stated failure tolerance, because these summaries do not measure how often a run fails. Model cards do not report how often the runs of a recipe fail, although whoever runs the training is best placed to count them, while those who rely on a retrained model bear the cost of a failed run. To report this failure probability directly, we propose recipe cards, an addendum to model cards that documents the model recipe behind a checkpoint. A recipe card states the bar and the tolerance and who chose them, reports how many runs are made and how many of them miss the bar, gives an upper bound on the failure probability, and warns when this bound exceeds the tolerance. Recipe cards record who set and who accepted this risk, and let deployers and regulators state acceptance criteria for retrained models.

papers.title: Neural Memory Orchestration

Heuristic prefetchers in the kernel handle stride-like and temporally clustered patterns well but degrade sharply on the irregular, data-dependent access streams typical of these workloads. An eBPF collector observes page faults on the target host, a transformer predictor (OverNet) runs on network-attached inference hardware and emits future page addresses, and a kernel-resident enforcer materializes those pages into the target's address space before they are demanded. OverNet encodes fault sequences through per-instance ordinal ranks over deltas, which lets a single trained model serve any target process without retraining. papers.title: Improved Leverage Score Sampling for Constrained Active Linear Regression
papers.summary: In this paper we study active learning for constrained linear regression. This problem arises in many scientific and engineering applications, and randomized leverage score sampling provides a powerful method to solve it. However, existing leverage score methods ignore the constraint or encode it through ridge regularization, suffering unfavorable query complexity for anisotropic constraint sets. We propose ellipsoid-regularized leverage scores, where we approximate the constraint set by an outer ellipsoid and use its shape matrix to bias sampling toward directions that matter under the constraint geometry. We prove that the query complexity is governed by an anisotropic effective dimension $d_{\text{eff}}(C)\le d$. With appropriate parameters, $O(d_{\text{eff}}(C)\log d/\varepsilon^2)$ queries suffice to return a point in $C$ with objective value at most $(1+\varepsilon)$ times the optimum. This bound can substantially improve on the standard leverage-score bound, since anisotropic constraints can make $d_{\text{eff}}(C)$ much smaller than $d$. For convex constraints, we improve the dependence on $\varepsilon$ from $1/\varepsilon^2$ to $1/\varepsilon$. We also prove two lower bounds: first, the $d/\varepsilon^2$ dependence is unavoidable without convexity assumptions on $C$, and second, in some regimes, the effective dimension dependence $d_{\mathrm{eff}}(C)/\varepsilon$ is necessary for ellipsoidal constraints. papers.title: A Systematic Analysis of a Small Optimal Subspace for Physics-Informed Neural Networks: $n$-DAS $\subset \mathbb{R}^p$
papers.summary: The search for a low-dimensional subspace that governs neural network training has been a persistent goal in optimization. To expose this structure under the hardest conditions, we use physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) as a testbed: differential operators from the parabolic, elliptic, and hyperbolic classes induce severely ill-conditioned, anisotropic loss landscapes. papers.title: Towards Generalizable Reasoning: Group Causal Counterfactual Policy Optimization for LLM Reasoning
papers.summary: Large language models (LLMs) excel at complex tasks with advances in reasoning capabilities. We then construct token-level advantages from this reward and optimize the policy, encouraging LLMs to favor reasoning patterns that are process-valid and counterfactually robust. papers.title: Same Rank, Different Needs: Rethinking LoRA Redistribution in Federated Learning

papers.title: A Matching Lower Bound for Online Smooth Calibration

papers.summary: Fairness audits treat a trained model as a fixed decision function, but the arithmetic that evaluates it is part of that function. This study holds the model, records, threshold and audit code fixed and varies the numerical execution contract in two tiers. Tier 1 changes only how products and sums are computed, with the serialized weights byte-identical, and is the causal test of arithmetic. Tier 2 runs reduced-precision deployment configurations (BF16 compute, FP8 and 8-bit weights), which can also round weights and change engines and kernels, so its effects belong to the configuration. It audits three tabular model families and two open-weight language models (4B and 24B parameters) on four public tasks, including hospital readmission, on CPUs and GPUs from NVIDIA, AMD and Apple. Tier 1 changed decisions near the threshold, and which ones depended on the GPU and its software stack, but no verdict under the prespecified, unweighted tests. Tier 2 configurations changed more decisions and some diagnostic verdicts, but no four-fifths verdict. Serving the 24B model with vLLM FP8 selected 54% of people rather than 45% and passed an employment-status audit by sex that its strict FP32 reference failed: its demographic-parity and equalized-odds gaps fell from 0.0567 and 0.0515 to 0.0417 and 0.0394, against a diagnostic tolerance of 0.05. At the reference's selection count FP8 failed demographic parity, and no reading gave its equalized-odds change a paired interval excluding zero. The declared audit depends on the configuration; FP8 is not shown to be fairer. At the frozen thresholds, every pass-fail verdict a configuration changed had a sampling interval containing its criterion. It proposes an audit stability protocol in which the auditor declares contracts, groups, weights and tests before scoring and records each verdict's range over them apart from its sampling uncertainty.

papers.title: Distilling a Geospatial Foundation Model into Compact Surface-Water Segmenters

papers.title: Tangent incompleteness under coupled image transformations: margin reconstruction and decision consequences
papers.summary: Can accurate responses to individual geometric image transformations recover their combined effect on a classifier's decision? For identity-aligned bilinear resampling, coordinatewise assembly may fail at first order. Projecting the implemented transformation onto a fixed logit-margin gradient, we derive a linear term plus signed absolute-value ridges. An exact even--odd identity and ridge-cancellation conditions characterize the missing information. Under independent parameter laws, a noncancelling off-coordinate ridge obstructs even unrestricted additive fits. The coupled correction has $O(s^2)$ projected error, versus a possible $Θ(s)$ axiswise defect; transfer to realized network margins requires local smoothness. Projected RMS errors fall by 82.96% on CIFAR-10 and 82.38% on ImageNetV2 relative to axiswise assembly; realized fixed-pair margin RMS errors fall by 39.75% and 42.73%. The representation prospectively identifies nine strict nonadditive network-margin sign configurations and permits exact minimization of a three-parameter threat surrogate, with conditional selection-regret guarantees. In an independent CIFAR-10 search, coupled-selected transformations uncover 51 top-1 changes versus 41 for axes. On 256 independent ImageNetV2/ConvNeXt-Tiny images and 16,384 transformed decisions at the prespecified scale $s=.40$, multiclass top-1 flip-prediction errors fall from 11.97% to 10.23% (paired improvement 1.74 percentage points; 95% interval [0.93, 2.61]). Directional finite differences are slightly more accurate (10.00%) at higher measured model-construction cost. These results connect first-order sampling interactions to margin reconstruction, decision prediction, and threat selection, without claiming finite-scale network certification.

papers.title: When Do LLMs Model the Right Target? Problem Formulation in High-Stakes Risk Prediction
papers.summary: Generative AI is increasingly used to assist with data science tasks, yet fundamental questions remain about its ability to correctly formulate analytical problems. We investigate how well large language models (LLMs) can formulate prediction problems when developing models for high-stakes decision making. We focus on one particular challenge to validity: decision dependency, which arises when historical decisions affect observed outcomes. We evaluate this aspect of problem formulation in LLM-generated code and explanations across child-welfare, healthcare, and employment settings, using 11 models from OpenAI and Anthropic and seven prompt conditions. We assess whether the LLM-generated code implements a procedure appropriate for estimating the intended outcome under the study's assumptions and whether the explanation acknowledges decision dependency. We find that LLMs do not reliably address decision dependency without guidance in the prompt. When prompts specify the target, the assumption needed to estimate it, and the estimation procedure, target-aligned implementation reaches 99-100%. Among frontier models, a simple prompt description of how decisions affect outcomes appears sufficient to elicit target-aligned implementation. Some responses also acknowledge decision dependency without addressing it in their code. Our findings suggest that analysts should not rely on LLMs to correctly formulate prediction problems without explicit methodological guidance and careful review. We propose validity-centered guidelines for LLM-assisted predictive modeling, covering prompt formulation, validation of the target and estimation procedure, and identification of key assumptions. Establishing validity is a necessary early step in evaluating whether to deploy a predictive model in a high-stakes setting, but deployment requires weighing broader ethical, institutional, and practical considerations.

papers.title: Perplexity Ranks Activation Quantisers but Understates What They Remove
papers.summary: Four-bit activation quantisation of language models is usually tuned and compared by perplexity. We ask what that misses, and find three things. First, perplexity gets the order of quantisers right but the size of their damage wrong. Across four models it ranks 33 of 34 pairs of settings correctly by closed-book QA loss, yet a 6-16% rise in perplexity comes with a 10-23% drop in QA accuracy, and the lost facts are mostly rare ones. Second, the ranking only holds while the quantisation error acts like random noise. Without rotation, rounding small values to zero deletes part of the signal, and this hurts in-context retrieval far more than noise of the same size would. The crest factor of the quantiser's input (its peak-to-average ratio) helps tell the two cases apart. Third, rotating in blocks, the usual workaround when a layer's width has no ready-made Hadamard matrix, can land a model in between and leave outliers behind; 10 of 42 popular open models have such a width. A full-width Hadamard exists for every such width we found, costs about the same, and on Qwen3-4B halves the closed-book TriviaQA loss (0.112 to 0.060, over three rotation seeds). We recommend reporting a knowledge-heavy task alongside perplexity, and rotating at full width wherever blocks leave an input outlier-heavy.

papers.title: What Interpolators Store and What They Express: An Information-Theoretic Framework for Benign Overfitting and Label-Free Model Selection
papers.summary: Overparameterized learners can fit noisy training labels perfectly and still predict well, which neither classical complexity measures nor information-theoretic generalization bounds explain. We develop an information-theoretic framework that separates two things an interpolating learner does with its sample: storage, the information the trained model retains about its training labels, and expression, the information about the sample that reaches its predictions at fresh inputs. We first characterize the ideal model: for a loss l, the least complex l-sufficient representation is the Bayes act, whose entropy is the minimal sufficient complexity; this generalizes, and corrects, an earlier "lossless maximal compression" view of boosting. We then show that every interpolator stores exactly nH(Y|X) bits of label noise, so storage, and bounds built on it (including CMI bounds), cannot tell interpolators apart. Expression can: excess risk is bounded above and below by the expressed information V, the entropy over training samples of the prediction at an input, plus a modal-bias term, exactly so for binary labels. Benign overfitting is therefore vanishing expression, a picture that covers nearest-neighbour rules, averaging, minimum-norm least squares and double descent, and that links V to classical bias-variance decompositions and to model disagreement. Finally, V gives a model-selection criterion that needs no held-out labels. Among overparameterized learners on 15 noisy datasets, V estimated from two disjoint halves has 60% less regret than holdout validation at the same cost and matches 5-fold cross-validation at a quarter of its cost; at matched cost it also beats selection by conditional mutual information. We characterize when it fails and give remedies. Code: https://github.com/nnikolaou/GLMC

papers.title: Two is better than one: optimizing binary rating scales for online platforms
papers.summary: Online platforms often struggle with inflated, uninformative user ratings. This issue can be mitigated by better design of the data collection mechanism, for example through changing the phrasing of user questions. Previous work optimizes a single rating scale to best distinguish the inherent qualities of items under binary feedback. In this paper, we demonstrate the power of utilizing different rating scales for different users. First, we show that a designer can always split a single rating scale into two to improve item rankings. Next, we formally characterize the optimal design of multiple scales as a series of 0-1 step functions whose threshold values are evenly spaced. Finally, we consider an adaptive model where subsequent rating scales can depend on the responses from previous users and items are ranked by their full sequence of responses, and show that adaptivity leads to exponentially greater distinguishing power. All in all, our theoretical results show that using multiple rating scales significantly improves item rankings on platforms.

papers.title: Systolic Linear Attention: Co-Designing Tile-Grouped Gated Delta Attention for TPUs
papers.summary: Gated-delta linear attention layers such as Gated DeltaNet (GDN), Kimi Delta Attention (KDA), and GDN-2 are tuned for GPUs, where small tensor-core tiles and fast vector registers make unpacked heads, per-channel decay rescaling, and per-value-head chunk solves cheap. On Google TPUs, which concentrate compute in wide $256 \times 256$ systolic matrix units backed by a slower vector unit, direct ports leave half of each matrix tile padded (for $d_k = 128$ heads) and repeat decay rescaling and chunk solves across every value head. We present \textbf{Systolic Linear Attention (SLA)}, which reshapes gated delta attention around the matrix unit by widening keys to $256$ and sharing both keys and scalar write gates $β_t$ across grouped value heads ($R\times$ fewer chunk solves), grouping decay gates into four $64$-channel tiles, and fusing exact FP32 block-doubling chunk inversion and its backward reuse inside one on-chip kernel. With exact chunk inversion on TPU v7x, $2$-stage \texttt{SLA-R4} (four value heads per key head) runs $2.1\times$--$2.6\times$ faster than open-source MaxText KDA and $1.4\times$--$2.4\times$ faster than open-source Tokamax KDA, while using $49\%$--$61\%$ less temporary high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Across a $2{,}048$-chip TPU v7x pre-training study of sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models from $6.5\text{B}$ to $63.1\text{B}$ nominal parameters, SLA trains $11\%$--$24\%$ faster than MaxText KDA ($4\%$--$21\%$ faster than Tokamax KDA), matches KDA perplexity on three paired seeds at $12.5\text{B}$, and stays within $3\%$ at other scales.

papers.title: Error accumulation in reverse diffusion with an imperfect score: beyond path-space analyses
papers.summary: Diffusion modeling is a popular method of sampling from a complex, high-dimensional distribution $p$ using learned approximations of its (noised) score functions. Generating a single sample requires simulating the reverse diffusion process, which requires many queries to the learned scores. Thus, a priori, the learning errors can easily compound. Indeed, in existing theoretical analyses, the sampling error (as measured in total variation distance to $p$) accumulates polynomially with the horizon of the stochastic process. This is a consequence of bounding the error of the output law by the error of the law of the entire reverse diffusion path. In this paper, we demonstrate that by circumventing the "path-space" analysis, the error accumulation of the diffusion sampler can be mitigated when $p$ satisfies a Poincaré inequality. Moreover, we achieve this result as a special case of a broader framework that applies to any distribution $p$, but relaxes the error metric from total variation distance to a weaker metric capturing all sample statistics that do not "witness" the multimodality of $p$. We then zoom out from analyzing the diffusion sampler to the information-theoretic question: given a learned score with some error bound, how accurately can we identify $p$? We show that, for any given bound on the Poincaré constant of $p$, the diffusion sampler already nearly achieves optimal total variation error.

papers.title: Isthmus: Bridging Supervision Islands Restores Uncertainty and Stability in One-Step Flows
papers.summary: One-step flow maps are increasingly used as posterior samplers, where the point of sampling is the uncertainty that the samples carry. We find that the one-step sampler loses this uncertainty and becomes less stable. Compared with multi-step samples of the same network, its samples lose variance and decorrelate. Supervising the one-step jump directly makes this worse; the samples collapse further toward the conditional mean and break down when training is extended. We trace both failures to the locations where training places its pairs of start and end times. Only pairs on the diagonal of the time triangle receive targets from data, and the pair used for one-step sampling is either left unsupervised or supervised on an island, a set of pairs that the self-consistency identity does not connect to the diagonal, where the objective neither determines the one-step map nor anchors its training. We bridge the island with an isthmus, which places 5% of the training pairs along the whole edge of the triangle that joins the one-step pair to the diagonal. The error of the one-step map is then bounded by the self-consistency residual along this edge. With the network, the loss and the inference code unchanged and at no added cost, the isthmus improves one-step sampling across several flow-map objectives, in MRI reconstruction, face inpainting, and unconditional generation on CIFAR-10 and ImageNet 32x32. On brain MRI, it restores one-step calibration to 0.96 and the correlation with multi-step samples to 0.93; both vary far less across seeds, and the agreement holds when training is extended to three times its length.

papers.title: Label-Free Role-Aware Segmentation of Classroom Recordings: Recovering the Teacher from Transferable Structure
papers.summary: How much the teacher talks and when are among the most informative and costly-to-measure signals of teaching. Yet, classroom audio is among the most sensitive data an AI system can process: recordings capture minors and fall under GDPR, preventing raw audio from leaving the recording device. papers.title: Training Autoregressive Language Models on Rounded, Bounded, and Censored Numerical Labels via Exact Likelihood
papers.summary: Numerical labels often specify a set of possible values: a measurement is rounded, a laboratory test reports only a bound, or a program is stopped at a timeout.
